132: new delhi, 28 september 2026: in a major blow to the ongoing agitation against chief election commissioner gyanesh kumar for alleged abuse of authority and election irregularities, and manipulation of voter rolls through sir, the delhi police denied a delegation of prominent activists permission for a people’s protest regarding the same on gandhi jayanti, 2 october 2026 at the jantar mantar road. this development has come hot on the heels of the cockroach janta party receiving a similar denial for their protest call in shivaji park, mumbai on sunday. “such tactics to suppress citizens’ voices are unacceptable. if we are denied the right to protest, cjp will launch a jail bharo andolan in mumbai on gandhi jayanti,” cjp founder abhijeet dipke wrote on x announcing the alleged denial of permission. the self described delegation, including prominent activists like aisa president neha bora, psephologist yogendra yadav, retired du professor nandita narain, and supreme court advocate prashant bhushan among others, remain steadfast in their intention to take the streets on 2 october. “show up in large numbers, especially those whose names have been struck off,” said nandita narain. “the media has been really brave, and more and more people are speaking up,” she said, in reference to the recent series of investigative reports by journalist ritika chopra for the indian express that has brought the chief election commissioner under fire for allegations of intentional cover-up of procedural violations by the body. very important protesters at 3 pm, the mic away). after making his apologies to the press for being unable to speak at length, yadav quickly exchanged positions with bhushan, who exited the station right after yadav went in, his security of it entirely.”
130: as a political student, activist, researcher, future advocate, an officer of the court and what have you, who has been protesting almost ceaselessly since 2023, the jantar mantar protest site has over the years been to me akin to a second home. through the years of my higher education, between home (in the more traditional sense) and university, jantar mantar became my most frequented haunt in delhi, where i was born and have lived all my still (hopefully) nascent life. from my college in the outskirts of ncr, i’d make the hours-long journey inward every weekend for a new cause: sometimes for women’s issues, sometimes over the labour codes, sometimes for political prisoners’ release; over land grabs and corporate loot, against unjust laws and for more just ones… all things civil and political. sometimes, i would hang around with comrades over suttas and chai to kill time before our demonstrations began, then go help set up shop or wait for the inordinate 1-hour delay. the anatomy of the student protest has a simple and predictable design: slogan, speeches and song, underscored by that feeling of camaraderie and togetherness with people one may have “antagonistic or non-antagonistic” contradictions with. this is particularly true of jantar mantar protests, the ones within the demarcated protest elsewhere, we’d almost certainly be immediately dragged and detained without warning, sometimes “kindly” (as kind as you can perceive the police to be while they are dragging you off of public sites of resistance and passivity). the detained evenings would be spent in some far-off police station at the very border of the city (bawana, kapashera, narela being favourites of the delhi police in terms of remoteness) and then wait till the night, when we would exert enough pressure to all be “allowed” to leave. in the period of 3 and a half years i’ve been around student activist spaces, i’ve observed detentions and the threats thereof to have become much more frequent and brutal. so much so that for a point in time, it even became impossible to protest in the real senses of the word. to protest in a public site would mean a sea of bureaucracy in terms of getting permission (or choosing not to) and mobilising,only to prepare for the almost definite eventuality of detention. on the better days, when the protest of the week occurred as intended rather than being dramatically yet unceremoniously shelved thanks to someone or the other being “detained out of sight”, i'd spend my evenings reading, discussing and strategising with “comrades”. my romance with so-called progressive student and political organisations, sordid and sensational, ended in justifiable estrangement on my side: after speaking out on what have now become my well-contentified experiences in the organised left, i faced still more patriarchal violence (sexual, physical), debasement (even from those groups that seemingly took an anti-rape stance “for” me) and determined, relentless, and passionate slander that continues to follow me to this day. but through all that and past it, my relationship with protest never ended, neither within my university (which thankfully, i recently graduated from), nor outside it. i remained vocal in the civil and political rights arenas, and showed up to protests nonetheless to the best of my ability. the protest against dharmendra pradhan on 20th july, called for by cjp and other associated organisations/groups, in this context, was markedly distinct from any other i’ve been a part of at jantar mantar till date, so much so that i felt it deserved my intellectual consideration beyond its political demands and strategic deconstruction. 20th july was unique in two key ways: first, the broader mass-based demands and outreach (as well as relatively lesser state-repression on a demand that struck the hearts of the “educated middle class”) meant the potential to grow into a mass movement, as opposed to smaller, much repressed, seldom permitted left-protests i’d most often participated in. second, in the overt misogyny i encountered at the site of protest, making me reconsider the mass-movement’s own understanding of its women constituents and their struggles. while i have my own opinions and ideological critiques of the cjp and this movement, i have put those aside in this essay to offer a reflective account of what i experienced at the protest, as a female activist. this article then contextualises my ideologies and affiliations with the left, and how my perspective evolved (whether for better or for worse, is left for the reader to decide) through these two specific lenses: a treatise on police brutality and the misogynistic abuse often invisiblised within protests. on the day of the protest, i left home around 7am, though the protest was beginning at 9. the indian state, which routinely shows up with batons, 20 or so “riot control” (detention) buses, and hundreds of police personnel to ostensibly secure protests by left-leaning organisations that optimistically gather downwards of 50 odd students on average, was more than satisfactorily prepared for the hordes of people who showed up to the call, students from across disciplines from all over the country, youngsters preparing for competitive exams, members of other ongoing resistances showing solidarity, job-goers, and everyone in between; an unusual combination of men, women, and quite a lot of children (from toddlers to teenagers) in the mood for revolt. it was so well-prepared in fact, that all routes to jantar mantar were blocked by the morning. as i walked the winding roads into the heart of central delhi toward the protest site (having taken an auto as far as it would go), i started getting calls from friends and comrades telling me that exits had been closed at the metro stations nearest to jantar mantar, trapping them inside, or skipping over stations entirely. i was supposed to be at the protest with a few other women who were there for the first time, not to the jantar mantar protest site, but to any protest at all. they’d indeed picked an interesting and unforgettable one for their first. i told my friends to meet me at bangla sahib, and from there we walked, following the maps we had (fortunately) downloaded ahead of time. cellular networks had, of course, already been suspended in the area, rendering our phones virtually useless. when my friends expressed shock at the internet shutdown, my internal (and partly external) monologue was fraught with cynicism: of course, this had happened. did the people of india not realise that just as the state had been doing for years in kashmir, manipur and other parts of the country, push come to shove, it wouldn’t refrain from doing anywhere and everywhere else, even the national capital? it wouldn’t refrain from, say, shutting down the internet when it came to masses gathering at jantar mantar, however protected the educated, white-collared sections of those masses of new delhi may think themselves to be?! i would find myself mentally revisiting this retort all through the day, as the state reminded us that the national capital, indeed, was not immune to its usual fascistic war machinery designed to be utilised against its own citizens: 12-gauge ‘pellet’ shotguns, chemical warfare, and lathi charges included. but my retorting voice, of course, grew weaker as the day progressed, coughing through walls of tear gas, ill-advisedly rubbing my eyes before washing them clean, or comforting a bleeding friend. i realised, slowly, over the day, that my unique experience in the group of being both accustomed and limited to spaces of marxist-leninist activism had made me “used to” police violence, normalised it in my mind as something that does happen all the time, and happens worse where the cameras are systematically never pointed, more on that later, whilst simultaneously leaving me unprepared for it allow me to explain: i’d been at the receiving end of police lathis before, been detained earlier, and marched despite orders not to march by the authorities. (after all, should a protest against an authoritarian, fascist state be done with its permission?) while fear was a slight ember flickering now and then through these dog days; the fuel of ideological commitment and belief in my comrades allowed me to be certain that even if i weren’t to be safe, were to be arrested, there would be people standing for me, as i would for them. my experiences with the left in the past year or two (which will be briefly elucidated upon in the second half) made me realise that perhaps not everyone is in the same struggle, for the same reasons and with the same incentives. further, as part of my ideological “upbringing” i’d led myself to believe and had been led to believe that with my “privilege” at least public protest would not be a site of death for me (bodily harm, i was fine with as a cost to pay for resistance). my estrangement with the organised left and the realisation that i may as well have been wrong in my latter supposition was a big wake-up call. on 20th july, months after this estrangement, i was not prepared for the events of the day. as it unfolded on myself and others, the delhi police’s brutality on 20 july 2026 took me wholly by surprise. we broke two-three barricades and were at the front of the crowd nearing parliament street, when the first direct confrontation with the police happened. the anti-riot squad stood in line faced towards us, lathis in their hands, their “anti-riot” shields up, helmet-visors drawn; we found ourselves unable to push past. so, we sat on the ground in front of them while we tried to figure out how to proceed. this was right in front of a line of barricades we’d just crossed, sandwiched between them and the state’s hired, official goons blocking our way, decked in full, militant glory. for good measure, i could also see two water-cannon wielding truck-like vehicles and several police buses blocking the route ahead by sporadically being placed across the middle and both sides of the oncoming road. the police began lathi-charge. everyone seated got up in a flurry. i reached to grab the hands of both the comrades i was with, assuming the crowd would use its inertia to push ahead past the attacking police. but, the police pushed us behind, by brute force, and the crowd behind pushed zealously ahead. those of us at the front, pushed in both directions, and closely sequestered into a few spaces, started falling. i used my quick-mindedness and memory from past lathi-charges to quickly take off my glasses and hand them one of the women with me, the message (i hoped) apparent: “don’t let them break, i am blind without them.” then, i felt my feet shifting against my will, just as i was twisting back to grab my friend’s hand. i fell down, and a stampede erupted around me. my nose pushed into the road; everything around me went black. i could hear people shouting above. i felt the air escape my lungs and i felt myself struggling to breathe. for a milli-second, a thought flashed into my head, a feeling of terror i haven’t been able to shake away still: “i am going to die in a stampede at jantar mantar.” the next second i started screaming for help, bloody murder, english-hindi a mix, hoping that someone would pull me out. i’d been stuck in semi-stampede situations caused by police at protests while they attempted to detain peaceful protesters before, but never a stampede-like attack where i thought i’d actually die. eventually, someone heard my cries and pulled me out. i found my friends, lying on the ground between people, but at least their faces were upright. the friend i’d handed my glasses to was holding them up above the fallen crowd in an attempt to save them from wreckage. i am nearly blind without my glasses but that purple speck above the crowd helped me note where my friends were and i called them and we rushed to the side, to the concrete pavement, where i heaved and almost cried trying to catch my breath. a police officer with his lathi soon came to get the “pavement sitters” who’d escaped the lathis and were mostly injured, and a few crying, women, and began a lathi charge on them too. eventually, somehow, this crowd made its way past this first lathi-charge into the second, which happened right outside the lic bank building, a few steps behind the parliament street police station, and a few steps in front of the old court building. here, i was separated from my friends, and faced a lathi charge alone, after getting stuck beneath two bikes at the side pavement while trying to escape another delhi-police orchestrated stampede. this was the first lesson i learnt that day: my experience as an activist who’s seen police brutality as a normal, everyday aspect of life, be it as a student, as a citizen or as an aspiring lawyer who works on prisoners’ rights, had in fact served only to desensitise me from the reality of it. this is not to say that police brutality is not a normal, everyday truth. let me tell you that police brutality is omnipresent in our justice system. it gets worse, deadly and much less reported or even recognised when the ones at the receiving end are not educated, financially privileged, caste-hindu, rights-knowing student activists. but as such, somewhere, i’d come to not only see it as a given cost of protesting, of speaking up in a state that is undoubtedly fascist, but also accept it. after i escaped the bikes and rejoined my friends, i still continued to draw comparisons to other parts of the country where state-sponsored violence of the same degree and worse has not only been happening for decades, but is the norm. since the inception of this “independent” country, certain communities and certain places (where the cameras stay curiously absent) have paid, pay and will for the foreseeable future continue to pay for their resistance (if not their existence ) with blood, breath, and freedom. but underneath those truths were two lucid, necessary recalibrations: 1) even if it wasn’t me that day; even if, due to my various socio-political privileges or chosen methods of advocacy and resistance, i’ve been led to believe it will never be me; anyone can die at the hands of the state. 2) police brutality has a cost: at best, the mental and physical well-being of those who face it, and at worst, incarceration, disappearance or death. and regardless of who is at the receiving end of it, that cost should never be paid. beyond the cynicism towards the protesting “middle class”, the caste-hindus who showed up when it came to them, but never against fascism the many, many times that it’s been mutinied against in this very city (the farmers’ protest, the caa-nrc movement, the longstanding demands for nta-nep’s demolition or the implementation of the manual scavenging act or the rohith act), or even the leadership of this protest that distanced itself from student political prisoners such as umar or sharjeel that i’d carried with me on the morning of the 20th, i felt something else. if every one of us who took the streets that day, some for the first time, saw the violent realities of this state firsthand as i had, i wondered if we might still come to stand against violence elsewhere and everywhere. the cynicism i’d internalised due to my particular experiences in the left began to feel misguided. i felt, after a long time, optimistic. i felt hope. the second distinguishing factor i experienced in the protest was the inescapable, evident, suffocating (way more so than the literal suffocation of the crowd) patriarchy. now, i am no stranger to patriarchy in places one imagines would be “better”, “less patriarchal”, “less violent” to women.(i say “less” instead of “non” deliberately, i was aware that patriarchy is plaguing our society, economically and socially, to the extent that to fight it is to recognise its existence in everything, and hence, i didn’t expect it to be absent in a left space that has historically done a lot but never enough in its struggle against patriarchy) my own experience as a woman has proved to me that political spaces mobilising for emancipation of all kinds, too, are hotbeds of the culture they purport to hope to destroy. that the same pervasiveness that misogyny enjoys in a woman’s public life (university, profession, navigation of public spaces) and her so-called “private” life (family, partnerships, friendships), it enjoys in her political life: as an activist, as a member of an organisation, or as a citizen rising up against the state. that being said, one fundamental experience i’d had as part of ml spaces was that of the spatial liberation they offered: from having comrades to stand by me if i left home as an adult woman at times or for periods my family deemed undesirable, to the very public act of protest itself. occupying space as a citizen, from within my university to jantar mantar, spaces that have traditionally been denied to women, making speeches, sloganeering loudly, shouting and coming face to face with the literal armed forces of the state, are not challenges to indian women’s participation in the left, but incentives for it . and though the so-called “comrades” of liberal-progressive inheritence, male and female, may be patriarchal, may indeed be rapists or rape-enablers (an expansion of this is the subject of another essay, for another time), when we come to protests, be they at jantar mantar or anywhere else, we are equals. men and women, in the “leftist” public space, are equals. in fact, it is often the women and the afab (assigned female at birth) comrades who are gathering up in chains at the front of the mass during detentions and lathi-charges, it is them who are at the forefront of resistance. representation-wise, too, although left groups struggle with having women substantively occupy leadership, they play the numbers game well. most protests i’ve gone to where students have been the majority protesters, the number of men to women is staggering at 50/50, give or take, and rarely is there a substantive under-representation of the latter. that itself says a lot, for it takes innumerable fights with various forces that contend to control an adult woman’s life (but yes, the primary force in this case, is family) to even have women students venture out of their homes if not for “justifiable” reasons (college classes, tuitions, jobs). there, facing the threat of police violence (beatings, detentions, arrests) and moreover, doing so with the spectre of your family creeping closer, perhaps as the detention extends past 6 pm (illegally), and you are left dodging calls… it is indeed one commendable act of the left, that it provides a space for women as part of the organisation, the university, the citizenry, the publically raging mass, as part of the collective. (this liberatory aspect is evidently contradictory to its own misogyny, my analysis? protest operates as theatre, a political performance, where gender contradictions are put aside by all parties for a while, for the “larger cause”. the “equality” isn’t a complete lie, it is materially orchestrated and meaningful, yet it isn’t the full reality either. it hides the tensions “behind the scenes”.) in the left, a woman seeks and finds refuge as a person who is angry, as an entity moving through and resting (existing) in public spaces: as a citizen with a voice. the left treats her as a person as capable of taking a stance as the man standing beside her. there’s very little grace i’ll give to the left in delhi after my experience of what i would call “organised rape cults” within it (a subject for another essay), but this is the little grace i’ll extend. the left, in its aesthetics, and hence in its protests, allows women to frequent public spaces. it does so, much more limitedly for queer and trans persons, too (gender expression that is non-normative, ultimately, is taboo in certain left spaces too). i remember, as a young woman of 19, i first frequented delhi roads past midnight while wall-painting with a political organisation. as a young, sheltered girl, the left was my material escape into freedom: with years of ideology, reading circles, organising and engaging with many different groups i grew confident to handle myself in public spaces that are inherently anti-woman. every woman knows that the public sphere is not for us. we are taught that very early in our girlhood: “it is not safe for you to go out alone,” in certain localities, at certain times. we learn to avoid dark streets, isolated areas, lone treks. we learn not to loiter, not to be out in a public space unless we need to. (because why would you expose yourself to possibilities of violence when you don’t “have to”?) public transport is inaccessible, though many of us don’t have a choice. we have gotten well-accustomed to stares, catcalls and lecherous or (on a lucky day) judgemental glances being thrown our way on every street we walk through. strangers anywhere can approach and at best, morally police (and at worst, batter, rape, and kill us). the people we know, within the localities we frequent, may be just as much of a threat. if none of this prevails upon you as a woman frequenting a public space in a day, maybe you’ll be familiar instead with the benevolent version of this patriarchy: “well-meaning” men, sometimes women, coming upon you, informing you it’s not safe to go this or that way at this or that time, asking you personal questions, commenting benevolently on how your dress or way of walking, way of sitting is inappropriate, etc. the infringement never ends. with this reality, protests were comparative safe spaces to me so far. at least within a protest, i believed, those fighting for the same cause as me would not expose me, or other women, to that sort of patriarchy, at least not till the third act ends and the curtains fall. so imagine my surprise, on 20th july, when as i negotiated with the police along with other men and women on the “back end” of the protest site, to “allow” us to enter the designated area of protest, i heard a group of men commenting, “ kaafi ladkiyan aayi hai protest mei. ” (“ a lot of girls seem to have come to this protest .”). i chalked it down almost immediately to men not being used to women occupying public spaces in the same way they do, in such closeness as the protest (like all protests) required. as the day continued, the crowd became tired of an absent leadership, repeated calls by the police to comply and to stop the protest, and the sweatiness, discomfort and festering restlessness of a crowd of tens of thousands sequestered into less than half a kilometre of a cordoned off piece of road. me and my (female) friends pushed our way to the front, where in all our enthusiasm we reached right where the barricades and rapid action forces separated the protest site from the city outside it. i tried to push, break, and holler at them with other men, but eventually a few kindly told me, “ ma’am app dab jao ke bheed mai, aap idhar mat aao. ” (“ ma’am, don’t come into the crowd, you’ll get crushed . ”) these men tried to convince my friends to go to the sides of the jantar mantar protest site, next to “a wall near a park”. in the meantime, the protest had gotten sweaty, dehydrating, and suffocating. one person fainted in front of us, and we gave him water before his friends carried him away (hopefully to a spot with less of a crowd). the mostly male crowd at the barricades from where we’d been sidelined was tired and angry. some of these well-meaning men thought that the best use of their time in a protest against neet paper leaks and for a better, more just education system, would be to “help” women jump over the aforementioned wall so they could be somewhere with “less heat, less crowd”, whether they wanted to be or not. as we refused , a few men pushed us to the wall and vehemently started explaining why we should go to the other side. our explanation that we would much rather be in the suffocating crowd wasn’t enough, these men were so very worried that we’d get injured or harassed within the crowd, that they thought it imminent to harass and injure us themselves. as if things weren’t bad enough, i saw that the electric wires lining the wall’s fence were giving shocks to the men and women trying to jump it. luckily, i was able to use that as an excuse to escape my well-meaning tormentors. then, me and my friends found other groups of women to push through the crowds with, and stick as much as possible, with groups of women throughout, as we pushed across not one, not two, but three rows of police barricades layered across short distances. i’ve already narrated the police brutality that we faced. now let me focus on the searing brutality of the everyday-variety of patriarchy i encountered from the male protesters. example one has been narrated above, now for example two: a comment i heard a random man make to his friend as we were standing in the crowd near him. “ kisi ki ladki ko kuch hona nahi chahiye. ” (“ nothing should happen to anyone’s girl here. ”) this made me furious. here i was, labouring under the delusion that, being an adult and an emancipated woman, my fellow protestors saw me as human. but no, i was in the basest expression of patriarchy, “someone’s” ladki (i assume daughter/wife/sister-adjacent) to a significant portion of the swathes of men around me. i was to be “protected” only as someone else’s property. not a person, not a human, not an independent being, not a comrade standing for the same cause: a woman defined in my relationship to men. then there was this elderly sikh uncle. barricade number 4, after the lathi-charge and the near death stampede: we had convinced the crowd to let the women at the front, since we could see more female cops at the front, whom we’d be better equipped to stand against. it worked. the crowd made way for me and the women with me. this elderly sikh uncle though, kept commenting, “ aadmi aaye hue hai, toh hum apni auraton ko kyun aage karein? ” (“men are here, so why should we put our women at the front?”) a particular brand of protective patriarchy every engage peacefully, one demonstrator did raise the indian flag. however, it was quickly snatched away, and the crowd began chanting “bharat mata ki jai”; some also chanted “jai shri ram.” from that point, the mob’s behaviour became increasingly aggressive. water and mud were hurled at protestors from balconies above. some chanted “israel zindabad, palestine murdabad,” turning the space into a site of hostility and intimidation. eyewitness accounts describe rapid escalation and targeted harassment, particularly of muslim participants and women protestors. one demonstrator shared: “it went really south… a sanghi crowd formed instantly and began aggressive sloganeering. they cornered our muslim colleague and started harassing women. i saw men surrounding a female participant and shouting at her.” “it went really south… a sanghi crowd formed instantly and began aggressive sloganeering. they cornered our muslim colleague and started harassing women. i saw men surrounding a female participant and shouting at her.” - a demonstrator at nehru place on 19th july 2025. the police eventually arrived, but rather than addressing the aggression of the right-wing crowd, they demanded workers argue that while the company has constantly expanded its sales and profits, the workers who have made this possible have been left out in the cold with no security of employment and labour exigencies of work.” only 5713 permanent workers out of the total workforce of 34,918 enjoy the benefits and high salaries that the company claims to provide its workers. the company has been recruiting workers directly after school in the name of running an iti and conducting skill development, others are recruited as temporary workers (tw) for 7-month-long contracts, and many others as contract workers for similar tenures ranging from a few months to a couple of years. workers are promised to be called for another tenure after some time if they maintain full attendance and work directly in production and spend their entire time on only one or two stations, gaining no definite skills. non-permanent workers and terminated permanent workers unite to form a formidable force a movement for establishing their union initiated by maruti suzuki manesar workers in 2011 is remembered as one of the most militant and important trade union struggles in the country in the last few decades. the year-long agitation succeeded in forming an independent union of workers on march 1, 2012 but was soon sought to be crushed by the management with an outbreak of violence on july 18 of the same year. the company had terminated 1800 contract workers and 546 permanent workers without an enquiry on the pretext of the violence and 147 workers were jailed out of which 31 were convicted temporary workers in main production processes. while being a cost-cutting measure, such a labour regime also allows the company to maintain a very high work intensity, such that only the very young and able can manage, and which is unsustainable for workers after a few years. it has also allowed the management to scuttle the rights won by unions of the permanent workers, formed after numerous militant struggles. hundreds of unions were formed in the belt, and the salaries and benefits of permanent workers saw a sharp improvement after numerous historic struggles throughout the 2000s and especially after the 2011 strikes in maruti manesar. the covid lockdown saw many layoffs and shutdowns, marking a setback to the permanent worker’s unions which no longer have the same hold over production, nor the impulse for militant struggle. the brunt of production has been shifted onto young non-unionized temporary workers who till now had found little space to articulate their deep distress. afternoon, 30th january 2025: police assaults a young activist & threatens to detain him. asp virender warns journalists not to take pictures. image courtesy: mouli sharma for tve the anger 111: following is the official press release of the maruti suzuki asthayi workers sangh for their demonstration outside the dc office in rajiv chowk, gurgaon on the 10th of january 2025 , where thousands of workers from several states joined those in haryana, which has been the epicentre of the maruti movement since 2011. the agitation of non-permanent workers started on 5th january, and stands hand in hand with the already protesting terminated workers union, the maruti workers sturggle committee, which has been on an indefinite strike near the company's manesar plant since september 18th 2024. january 10, gurgaon: thousands of current and erstwhile non-permanent workers of maruti suzuki gathered at the gurgaon dc office to submit their collective charter of demands to the labour department challenging the illegal labour practices of the company. the workers have organised themselves under the maruti suzuki asthayi mazdoor sangh, launched on the 5th of january, 2025 in a mass meeting held at krishna chowk, gurgaon. the charter of demands was also submitted to the company management on january 9, 2025. the labour department has scheduled a tripartite meeting with the company management and the sangh on january 31, 2025. the demonstration also submitted a memorandum to the chief minister of haryana and declared a massive mobilization and workers march in imt manesar on the 30th of january. a working committee of non-permanent workers from different states and representatives from among the maruti terminated workers is leading the agitation. the workers have demanded an end to the reliance on various categories of temporary workers for regular production in all plants of the automobile giant. they are demanding permanent employment for work of a permanent nature, equal pay for equal work, hiring of temporary workers previously and presently employed by the company to all the plants as permanent workers including the new plant in kharkhoda, sonipat and ensuring useful and recognized training of maruti student trainees and apprentices. non-permanent workers arriving into the area for the agitation have been camping at the protest site of terminated maruti workers at the manesar tehsil near imt manesar chowk, seven kilometers from the company gate. “workers are not footballs to be kicked out at your whim!” sumit, a temporary worker from bahadurgarh gave the movement its defining metaphor of temporary workers being footballs kicked around from company to company. the image comes from his own 12 year long experience in the automobile industry where he has worked in the hero car plant in noida and the hero bike plant in manesar besides various stints in maruti suzuki. suzuki employs more than 34,918 workers out of which only 18% are permanent, 40.72% are contractual workers, 21.6% are temporary workers (tw), 21% are student trainees (mst) and apprentices. workers are trapped in an infinite cycle of hope and despair as the company hires them for short spans extending to seven months to one-two years and then releases them promising to call them again after a few months. trainee workers are first hired as tw1, of which around 10% are rehired after a year as tw2 and a handful are called as tw3. the same logic operates for contract workers who are called cw1, cw2 and cw3. this creates an extended relationship between the company and a massive pool of skilled labour kept in suspended and partial unemployment for years with short stints in employment at the convenience of the company. the massive pay gap between permanent workers receiving an average monthly salary of 1,30,000 and non-permanent employees who receive 18,000 to 30,000 is another major bone of contention for the workers. despite the main workload depending on this non-permanent workforce, there exists a great disparity in the facilities enjoyed by permanent and temporary workforces. a large part of the salary consists of incentives which are easily deducted for temporary workers on taking leaves, or fluctuations of production targets. twelve years after the manesar agitation, workers face the same issues. maruti suzuki management became infamous after workers of its manesar plant spent a whole year in agitation for the formation of their union in 2011-12. the agitation was sought to be crushed by a massive breakout of violence on july 18, 2012 leading to the death of a management executive from asphyxiation in the fire. the incident was followed by widespread police repression and the arrest of 117 workers of which the entire original union body was sentenced to life imprisonment. 23,000 permanent and contractual workers were terminated without an inquiry after the incident. at the root of the agitation was the grievance of unbearable work pressure, insufficient wages and widespread use of contractual workers in production. permanent workers terminated in 2012 have been sitting in an indefinite sit-in in imt manesar since october, 2024 and have been instrumental in the build up of the present agitation claiming that the present movement is a continuation of the demands which had prompted them to begin agitating for a union in the first place. the management had claimed that it had done away with contract workers after the agitation, and addressed the grievances of the workers. the present agitation reveals how these claims stand valid only for the small permanent workforce in the plant, whereas the majority of the workforce continues to be plagued by bad working conditions such as inability to take bathroom breaks, being marked as absent for a delay of mere seconds in signing into the plant, deduction of a sizeable portion of their salary for not achieving full attendance, only 7 mins for tea and half and hour for lunch within which workers have to walk for over a kilometer to go to the mess and come back. the sham of skill development every year thousands of youth are churned out of various maruti suzuki plants as student trainees and apprentices. they are admitted under the maruti suzuki iti program but are engaged in direct production, being made to work at the same station, turning the same nut and bolt for a year or two years depending on their trade and then released with a certificate which holds no meaning in the labour market. sandeep (age 25) is fighting a case in the haryana high court because he was refused recruitment in a haryana government job where his experience certificate from maruti was refused recognition because it mentioned no specific work experience. the company is a happy contributor to the government’s claim to generating thousands of new jobs every year. but the massive gathering of workers reveals the dark reality behind these claims, where all this employment is merely ephemeral, lasting not more than a few months. the claims of upskilling through the national employment enhancement mission are in fact just a façade to provide cheap skilled labour to companies like maruti suzuki. press release, maruti suzuki asthayi mazdoor sangh . contact: 9911258717, 9958426959, 9671705166, 9990115799, 9050073578. 110: following is hindustan times’ deputy national editor, dipankar ghose’s 18 part eulogy on x for bastar based journalist, mukesh chandrakar, who was found dead in a septic tank at the property of a construction contractor he had earlier exposed for corruption. ghose highlights the disproportionate risks faced by regional & independent journalists in india. 5th january 2025: how do you begin to write a tribute to a journalist, a friend, a brother? how do you describe him when nothing really contains him? the first time i met mukesh chandrakar was in december 2015, weeks after i had landed in chhattisgarh as the indian express reporter there. dipankar ghose is a wht scholar from the university of oxford. he is presently the deputy national editor at hindustan times. in 2015, he met mukesh while covering a story in bastar. image courtesy: weidenfeld-hoffmann trust, university of oxford there was a story in bastar, and i had reached bijapur, one of india's most dangerous places to report, with very little to go on. there i was, at the district headquarters, in a run-down press club building among a group of journalists eyeing me suspiciously. the suspicion of "national journalists" is warranted. very often, we climb on the shoulders of our regional colleagues, leave them to danger, or worse forget we know them. the story spot was deep inside the forests, some 80 kilometres away. i asked loudly, sheepishly, if someone would come with me tomorrow. by come with me, i meant take me. in that moment, i was helpless. there was only one voice that said "haan, kal chalenge aapke saath." i went back to the relative comfort of my hotel in jagdalpur. mukesh went to the mechanic shop to repair his motorcycle for what lay ahead. the next day, at the agreed 5 am, we met at the bijapur bus stop(there was no network except bsnl in bastar in 2015), and set off. he was young, but he was my first teacher in bastar. he taught me the dangers of relieving yourself on the sides of a freshly laid road,because that's where an ied would be. he taught me to stand up on the back of a bike to ensure that your muscles don't spasm under duress. we navigated paved roads, and then unpaved roads, and then no roads. carried the motorcycle across streams. waded through mud. he told me how to navigate a complicated world of hostile police, hostile maoists, and beleaguered people. it was an important story, and the state took note. but the byline said my name, not his. mukesh did this over and over again. not just for me, but for many others. it was on his back that the stories of bijapur, of lives lived in conflict, were ever told. for me, mukesh was the personification of bravery. i'm not going to pretend that in a universe where media organisations he worked for didn't even pay for his petrol let alone a stable salary, sustenance wasn't a problem, and therefore some wires weren't crossed. but mukesh loved journalism with a passion. when he was with you, nothing was impossible. he was always compassionate to people he reported on, always empathetic. he was rooted in bastar, but not limited by it. after a decade of jumping from one channel to the other, he realised organisations would never truly value its ground reporters in the region. he recognized the power of technology, and started bastar junction, a youtube channel that at last count has 162k followers. go to youtube now and watch his videos, and you will find more journalism than screaming television studios can ever offer. he reported from spots of attacks, crossed forests and mountains to get to victims of violence, reported from police camps, and from naxal camps. journalism in bastar has risks, and he bore them all. getting to a spot is more physically arduous, more dangerous than most can imagine. maoists threatened his life several times; the state threatened him when he exposed excess. he was often bullied by his own bijapur fraternity for helping "national journalists" but he never, ever wavered. it was him, and my other dear friend ganesh mishra, who risked their lives and went deep into the forests to rescue a crpf jawan abducted by maoists. but bastar claimed him. on december 24, mukesh reported on a shoddily built road in bijapur--an obvious case of corruption. the story caused an enquiry. a week later, mukesh was found dead, buried inside a septic tank in the home of the contractor that built that road. the last time i met him was during the chhattisgarh elections, when i spent the day with him and ganesh mishra. we reported, talked and laughed for hours. and then mukesh took me home because he had cooked some lunch for me himself. we laughed and lamented my distance from bastar, and friends like the two of them. his last message to me, in october, had the words "pata nahi kab mulakat hogi, par mulakat ka intezaar humesha rahega." i told him, "jald hogi mulakat." how does one begin to remember him? as a journalist? as a bridge to bastar? as the voice of those that would never be heard otherwise? remember him as them all. to me, he was mukesh chandrakar, my friend, my brother. go well, bhai. mulaqaat ka humesha intezaar rahega. dipankar ghose is a wht scholar from the university of oxford. he is presently the deputy national editor at hindustan times, and previously worked with the indian express. he is a three time ramnath goenka awardee, & received the prem bhatia award for journalism in 2020.
109: following is the official press release of the maruti suzuki asthayi mazdoor sangh (maruti suzuki non-permanent workers' union), whose founding meeting was held at saat fere vatika , gurgaon on sunday, 5th of january 2024. 5th january 2025 : in a significant move, more than three thousand erstwhile workers of maruti suzuki gathered for a mass meeting near krishna chowk in gurgaon on sunday, january 5th, 2025 in the founding general meeting of the maruti suzuki asthayi mazdoor sangh . many had travelled overnight to reach the venue from bihar, jharkhand, rajasthan, orissa and other states. the workers have all served in various temporary capacities at the three plants of the automobile manufacturer in gurgaon-manesar. a charter of demands was prepared, adopted and signed in the meeting today. the workers also issued a call to gather in an even greater number at the gurgaon dc office on january 10th to submit the charter of demands and make their presence felt before the labour department and the company management. the general meeting also elected a committee of representatives to coordinate its further activities. presently maruti suzuki employs 36,000 workers across its four plants, out of which a mere 17% are permanent and the rest are divided into various categories which include temporary workers 1 and 2, casual workers, apprentices, contract workers and student trainees. the entire production of the plants is dependent on this temporary workforce, whereas the role of permanent workers has been limited to supervisory roles at best. there exists a huge pay gap between permanent and temporary workers, with permanent employees drawing an average salary of 1,30,000 while temporary workers draw salaries between 12,000 to 30,000. temporary workers are recruited for a mere seven months at a time. student trainees form another significant category of the workforce who are engaged in full production in the name of apprenticeship and iti education, only to leave the plant after two-three years with a certificate that has no currency in the labour market. the charter prepared by the workers demands permanent employment for all workers engaged in a permanent nature of work. the workers have demanded the creation of 30,000 permanent posts in the existing three plants. they have also demanded that the recruitment to all these posts including those in the upcoming plant in kharkhoda, sonipat should be held primarily from among those who have previously worked in any maruti plant as temporary workers. in the meantime all temporary workers must be given a 40% pay hike and a ‘clearance amount’ equal to the difference in the salaries of temporary and permanent workers for every month of service in the company. with regard to the sham training process being conducted by the company, workers demanded that the government intervene to ensure that student trainees being recruited by the company are actually allowed to up-skill themselves and not be engaged as workers in the main production process. the meeting was organised in the wake of a demand notice submitted by the maruti suzuki struggle committee on behalf of various categories of temporary workers presently working in the four plants. the meeting also received active support and assistance from maruti workers terminated from the company in 2012. these workers have been agitating to be reinstated with back wages for their unfair dismissal and sitting in imt manesar in an indefinite sit-in since september this year. source: tve
108: the conference at the press club of india held on the 16th of october, paneled spokespersons of the many prominent workers’ protests across the country that have been absent from the mainstream media, & implored the public & press to acknowledge their struggle. senior supreme court adv. colin gonsalves and anjali deshpande, the latter being one of the few journalists to cover the maruti workers’ struggle when it began over a decade ago, were also present. 16th october 2024, new delhi: on wednesday afternoon at the press club of india, representatives from four of the country’s ongoing workers’ protests along with prominent journalists & activists organized a press conference to address the stark lack of media attention these movements are receiving in the mainstream news. the four movements in question are the maruti suzuki workers’ struggle in manesar, haryana; the samsung strike in sriperumbudur, tamil nadu; the dolphin and lucas tvs struggle in uttarakhand; and the darjeeling hills tea plantation workers’ struggle in west bengal. of these, only the samsung strike in tamil nadu has featured in the mainstream news, largely owing to the workers’ own effort to carry out independent reporting. maruti suzuki workers struggle, manesar, haryana: "chalo imt manesar!" beyond the distant movements of darjeeling, tamil nadu & uttarakhand, the movement that stood out most in the press conference – not only because two out of the four protests represented were part of it, resisting different parts of the same corporate machinery, but also because it was based right here in delhi ncr – was the maruti suzuki workers’ struggle in manesar. this protest is also tied to the dolphin and lucas tvs struggle in uttarakhand, as dolphin is a supplier of maruti, & both are cases of gross violations of labour laws for factory workers. on 18th july 2012, after an incident of caste-based discrimination between management & the then recently formed union spiraled out of control, 13 workers in maruti’s manesar factory were charged with crimes they did not commit, arrested & jailed for sentences of life. this is the incident that sparked the movement that spanned 10 years and 3 plants of maruti suzuki, resulting in the illegal termination of 2346 workers, the arrest of as many as 150 workers, & withheld dues of over 20,000. in 2017, 117 of the detained workers were acquitted and released, after wrongfully being jailed for several years. the continued resistance of the maruti workers – most of whom despite being acquitted carry with them the tag of ‘jailed worker’ & cannot find employment - has been a testament to their resilience, & their unceasing decade-long struggle finally resulted in the 13 jailed for life leaders securing bail in 2022. despite the dramatics of their story, media coverage of this 12-year-long battle has been negligible. a month ago, prior to the haryana elections, the workers resumed their strike through an indefinite st-in starting on the 107: the grounds outside jnu’s sabarmati dhaba have seen many a crowd with raised fists sloganeering for festival, protest, & the mutant cross between the two that is the union election; yesterday, they were raised in grief. g. n. saibaba ‘stubbornly refused to die’ for every day of his 3,592-day brutal incarceration since his arrest by the indian state on the 9th of may 2014, until he couldn’t anymore at the age of mere 57. in letters to his wife written from the solitary confinement of his ‘anda cell’ in nagpur central jail, he once wrote a poem that said, “the sad thing is, they don’t know how to kill me.” as of 12th october 2024, the sad thing is, they learned. new delhi, 14th october 2024: the unlawful activities prevention act, 1967 (recently amended in 2019 by the incumbent bjp government) is india’s primary legislation on ‘terrorism.’ it is widely regarded as a draconian law in dire need of revisitation because of its use of controversial legal overreaches such as increased investigative prerogatives, lowered guilt criteria, ambiguous language 1 , & perhaps most damningly, extended conditions on applying for & receiving bail. in may 2014, a 46-year man was charged under this act & quietly arrested in new delhi. the alleged terrorist was handled with appropriate secrecy needed for matters of national security; he was transported discretely to the airport & taken to nagpur in anti-landmine trucks full of commandos armed with high-tech weaponry, from where more trucks were seen escorting the prisoner to gadchiroli, where he would be tried 2 . marathi media quickly reported the big news – a hardcore & dangerous terrorist had been caught, possibly a maoist leader. this man was du’s beloved & revered professor, 90% disabled & paralyzed from the waist down since a childhood battle with polio, dr. gokarakonda naga saibaba. saibaba lost the use of his legs when he was only five years old. as his wife & comrade a. s. vasantha kumar i wrote to him through the walls of prison in 2022, ‘your legs were motionless, but your hands were your strength.’ as he breathed his last at 8:36 on the 12th of october, 2024, saibaba no longer had the use of his hands. they were taken from him years ago, after his arresting officers threw him into a police car, breaking both his wheelchair & his hands – the first of many abuses they would suffer during his disturbing & inhumane capture. the nerve damage from the fall would later grow into an infection that would render his hands barely usable. while they transported saibaba to gadchiroli, his wife was left in the dark. as she went to the local police station to file a complaint for her missing husband, g. n. saibaba’s hands had already begun to, slowly & painfully, die. seven months after his release from the nagpur central jail, where he was falsely incarcerated for over 10 years, on the 12th of october 2024, renowned professor & human rights activist dr. g. n. saibaba passed away. the next evening, a small group of people at jnu’s iconic sabarmati dhaba came together to do something enthusiasm cannot help with – grieve. photojournalist kandarp bhargav’s photographs document the necropolitics of not just a disabled academic’s institutional murder , but also those of another, quieter one still in progress. it is the murder of the academic apparatus of this country, one which in these photographs is being asked to organize & attend its own wake. on the banners behind the tennis court where the crowd eventually gathered & in the whatsapp forward stragglers who’d made up their minds last minute were toting around, the names given to the gathering varied. the big red banner nestled between the communist flags on the hedges called it the ‘red salute to comrade g. n. saibaba.’ the forward doing the rounds on people’s statuses called it a ‘public meeting’ remembering his legacy. the posters lined on a string stretched across the court read like a protest against the law, but the voices in the crowd sounded hesitant the way they rarely are at those, like they’re undecided which of the three they want this to be. hindu’s article the next morning about the event conveniently labeled it a ‘tribute by friends, professors & students,' which sounds - if nothing else - nice. “the event in itself was in solidarity with g.n saibaba and yet was a protest against the oppression of the authorities and the government. the meeting started with loud hails of anti-fascist sloganeering [which gave the idea of it being a protest]. eventually, several people gave speeches,” kandarp says, trying to describe the atmosphere of the meeting. perhaps, the first stage of grief has always been confusion. three days before saibaba’s death from a postoperative complication in a gallbladder surgery, industrialist & chairperson of the multibillion-dollar tata conglomerate, ratan n. tata passed away due to natural causes at the age of 86. people the world over being platformed by national & global media, particularly the government & laypeople of maharashtra, alongside social media users all across the globe were heartbroken over his death, with celebrities & politicians flocking either to x (formerly twitter) or to his state-sponsored last rites in mumbai to pay him their last respects. g. n. saibaba’s history with maharashtra & the state is just as rich as tata’s 3 , but not quite as wholesome. perhaps that is why the crowd at his makeshift ‘funerals’ like the one at jnu – or the ‘ real one ’ in hyderabad – was neither as diverse, as sad, or as newsworthy; nor the queue for it quite as long. “ratan tata was a business person who knew how to deceive struggling low purchasing power people of india, g.n saibaba [for the government and the masses] was a threat,” says kandarp, explaining why the sentiments of the masses are more attached to ratan tata than activists like saibaba. “as the state said, ‘saibaba's brain is dangerous. his thoughts are dangerous.’ so the mainstream media would never appreciate his struggle and resistance against authoritative oppression.” the words kandarp refers to here are those that were used two years ago when news of the reconviction & denial of bail to a 90% disabled professor with a steadily declining physical health after years of imprisonment spread across the country, as the court’s justification. “ the brain is more dangerous ,” said justices m.r. shah and bela m. trivedi in the supreme court of india, our highest authority of justice. it is a terrorist’s intelligence, not his physical capacity that threatens the ‘unity & sovereignty’ of a country; saibaba’s wheelchair & nerve-damaged fingers were hardly a reason to be careless. his mind worked fine. when asked who then showed up for the meeting, which was open to all, kandarp’s answer is unsurprising. “the poster itself mentions all the pro-left student organizations around the campuses of du and jnu [organizing it],” kandarp reminds us. “you are limited to your opinion ,” and so is your grief. 4 “the community of people grieving him today are the ones who share comradery and solidarity in the resistance against the oppression of government institutions – activists and professors from different universities who shared close memories of g.n saibaba. one of them was hem mishra.” this hem mishra, of course, is the jnu student who was among the five others jailed alongside saibaba in the uapa “maoist links” case. like saibaba, mishra was also released from jail & acquitted on all charges in march, more than ten years after he was first arrested. written to sanjay kak, from the high-security prison cell, nagpur, to the fellow netizen prisoners of the global virtual space, dr. g. n. saibaba, 24 march 2018. after the meeting at sabarmati, mishra would leave for hyderabad, where saibaba’s body rested at his brother’s residence before being donated to telangana’s gandhi medical college, to pay his last respects to the man he spent a decade with in hell. written to vijay kumar, based on the stories told by two prisoners who spent prison terms for petty crimes, dr. g. n. saibaba, 12th april 2018. “he would say that one day we would walk out of prison,” mishra would recall , at the makeshift funeral. “because we did nothing wrong. we raised our voices against injustice, for the rights of the people, for the rights of adivasis, dalits and all the oppressed in this country. we were, and are, fighting for a just cause,” he would say. but sunday night on the tennis court outside sabarmati, righteousness did little to soothe anyone’s raw conscience. a man with silver hair & grandpa glasses stood up against the weight of his shaking cane to remind those who'd come to listen of the legacy his friend left behind, one of endurance & resistance against authoritative oppression. a trade union worker described the distinctive empathy of saibaba’s politics, so grass-rooted that it would apply directly to the on-ground resistance of the trade union. and when the three long hours of speech & slogan came to a slow, hollow end, it was hardly their pride that stayed with kandarp on his metro ride home. “on my [journey back home], all that hooked me up was the thought of how the government is so afraid of students and such events that they totally record and monitor the spectators and the speakers.” in one of the videos kandarp took from the meeting, two security guards stand stock still with their hands behind their backs, quietly watching from the boundaries as students chant slogans in memory of saibaba & his fight against fascism. as the camera hovers over them for more than a second instead of moving past, one of them turns towards it, looking kandarp in the eye. less than a second later, he turns back. intimidation & surveillance from campus authorities at protests is far from new phenomena at places like jnu, but kandarp tells us it is on the rise. “the administration in public universities is restricting any vocal stands from students, be it study circles, meetings, or a protest, and all this has amplified post covid,” he says. “the government is so afraid of students and such events that they totally record and monitor the spectators and the speakers.” kandarp also criticizes the nep for trying to mechanize the education process, conditioning students out of their ability to think critically. “[they] try to put students in some machine learning structure and want to teach [them] the ideology the center is pleased with: promoting the culture of a certain religion and killing the idea of the secular nation. my experience with professors around delhi university has been the same.” three years ago, after being arrested under the false bhima koregaon conspiracy for which several activists were booked & jailed under the same charges that took away 10 years of hem mishra & g. n. saibaba’s lives (‘alleged’ links to maoist groups under uapa), 84 year old tribal rights activist, father stan swamy passed away while incarcerated as he was denied bail despite being critically diagnosed with parkinson’s. the same was done to saibaba & his fellow prisoners, of whom pandu narote succumbed to swine flu in 2022 while also still in jail. it seems that when it comes to the workings of the indian judicial & extrajudicial apparatus , idealogy is not the only thing they intend to kill. “g. n. saibaba’s death is a reminder that the pm’s vicious use of terms like ‘urban naxal’ has real consequences. he was only 57,” said ashish gawande, sharad pawar’s spokesperson for ncp, a day after saibaba's death 5 . “this is institutional murder.” “you had written, ‘just like how the state apparatus is sucking the life out of the people and the society, it is squeezing my body dry too. i do not know how much of myself will be left when i leave the prison.’ i too fear the same. even ablebodied people are not able to endure the harshness of prison life; it must be far worse for you. my biggest concern right now is your health, especially the fact that you have not received any medical treatment in the last four years. once you wrote to me that you were not sure how long you could survive in these conditions with an abject lack of medical attention. you said that we might hear the news of another stan swamy if no treatment is provided to you. whenever i think of these words, my mind goes to a dark place and a heaviness that does not leave fills my heart.” january 2022, a.s. vasantha kumari, translated from the telegu by rajendra babu arvini and p. varalakshmi as i sat down to edit this photo essay, amidst invitations to du’s own ‘public meeting’ of the same format & subject in the arts faculty, saibaba’s institutional & political haven while he taught english at ram lal anand till his unceremonious & insulting removal from the post in 2021 as a result of the war waged on his character by his own country, i found myself stuck on the image of a lone loudspeaker softly echoing the voices of the attendees’ organized grief. i thought about asking kandarp if saibaba’s own voice ever spoke out of that speaker at any point in the meeting, then remembered the circumstance & let it be. the thought has nagged at me through the writing of this article; a moronic, transhumanist variant of the worthless platitudes we give to each other when people die: they are alive in what they’ve left behind. remembering his eulogy for stephen hawking – another wheelchair bound genius who chose academic prodigality over hopelessness, & in the end was comparable to saibaba in little more than silhouette – i couldn’t stop imagining his computerised voice speaking gently from that speaker, being reminded everytime of why i already knew the answer to my question. it would be all too easy, for the same reason why it would be much too painful, to pretend he was there on that tennis court by proxy, because it would be akin to pretending he was still alive. despite the complete loss of use of his left hand, & near complete loss in his right, g. n. saibaba would write in prison. partly for lack of choice; after the state of maharashtra reinstated jail mulakats post the covid-19 pandemic, all phone calls were stopped. this was only a formal seal on what was already a black box of communication in the form of nagpur central jail, psychologically tormenting prisoners & their families by withholding news of even their medical conditions. but even when his letters had little hope of reaching their intended address, & even though by the end of the decade it would take him 2-3 days to complete a single page of writing because of the deteriorating state of his hand, saibaba wrote. he wrote letters to his family, though he was denied even doing that in his mother tongue, & each letter either way had to be arduously translated. he wrote back & forth to his wife, a bastardized memory of their youth where they exchanged pages upon pages of their young, hopeful love. he wrote to the court, afraid for his life in a prison that locked him up like an animal & forced him to beg for life-saving drugs & the dignity of not having to drag himself around by his elbows. he wrote to fictional characters & his students & colleagues to remind them where the real prison was; in our own moral decrepitude. he wrote to his friends . through excruciating pain, he never stopped writing. on october 26th 2017, in a letter to his wife, saibaba wrote a poem remembering the october revolution in russia a hundred years prior. it is this poem that opens the collection of his writings from prison which came out of it two years before he did, titled, ‘ why do you fear my way so much? ’ 6 the title calls on the reader the same, absurd association with saibaba’s shaking pen that the mainstream media tried to purport 8 years prior when he was first captured: fear. but saibaba was never the mastermind they were so intent on having us, asininely, believe. he wrote poetry on art & justice & blades of grass, and remembered the dates in history books. he was an english teacher, till the end, & his only crime was an undying smile & refusing to die when he was asked to. written to vasantha, remembering the october uprising of 1917, g. n. saibaba, 26th october 2017. in a pixellated, zoomed-in still from kandarp’s collection, his lens struggles to get a clean shot of three posters in a line behind the silver-haired speaker’s head. the first of them reads a slightly different version of the line – transformed either in translation or memory: ‘they don’t know how to make me die.’ i mull over the eccentricities of meaning & semantics, & my mind wanders back to the loudspeaker. to the speeches & interviews & papers, to the people and the places, and the book full of prison poetry he’s left behind. as of 12th october 2024, the state certainly figured out how to kill him, the way it killed stan swamy & pandu narote, & the way it is killing its own academia as we watch it happen. but maybe, it is worth believing, that it will never figure out how to make him die. kandarp is a 23-year-old journalism undergrad at the university of delhi. hailing from eastern up. kandarp is passionate about photography and filmmaking. he uses his art to address social issues, & currently works as an independent photographer. he & his work can be found @kandarpbhargav on instagram. mouli sharma is a scholar of religion at jamia millia islamia, and a freelance journalist from new delhi, india. she is a published photojournalist & illustrator, having been featured in the hindu college gazette, & the quarterly pink disco. she currently serves as the editor-in-chief of the student-run news site, the voice express , & as a literary editor for the digital lit-mag , the queer gaze.
106: collective delhi secretary sourya’s statement recounts the tata group’s long history of forceful land acquisition & human rights violations, calling out the selective memory & revisionist narrative of tata’s posthumous virtue being put forth by the media in the wake of his death. 13th october 2024, new delhi : with the demise of industrial giant & 5th generation heir of the tata group on october 9th, 2024, ratan n. tata, the late tycoon has quickly become a global symbol of ethical entrepreneurship & philanthropy, being hailed as a visionary by foreign governments & local critics alike. but in a world where mourning & condolence come tied to social conventions & speaking ‘ill of the dead’ is avoided like a totem cursed with the worst curses of them all (being frowned upon), it can become difficult to tell the grief apart from the spectacle. certainly it is safe to say, that when it comes to the press, grief is spectacle 1 . as vips spent the last 48 hours celebrating the life & mourning the loss of tata – who died of natural causes on wednesday morning at the age of 86 – to immense media attention, one side of the coin that has been wholistically ignored by mainstream as well as large parts of independent media is that of the tata group’s political history, one that is fraught with violence and controversy. in the cacophony of mournful obituaries & funeral telecasts 2 drowning out any and all counternarratives from the newssphere, one demographic that is sustaining a quiet, consistent voice of dissent, is the youth. whether through student representatives or through digital apparatuses 3 , the young left has held onto its views on tata, intent on highlighting the group’s bloody history. as the country’s press covers which celebrities were seen in attendance of tata’s (twitter) funeral, which 23 of his quotes make the best compilation, & writes a headline for every person – from a newspaper vendor 4 to amitabh bachchan – that can offer a quote of condolences for the tycoon, young journalists, digital media influencers, & left-wing student organisations in their infancy have been unflinching in their continued critique of the less picturesque aspects of the tata group’s evolution. this is the first of a series of articles that hopes to uphold, even if only microscopically, the desperate & delicate balance of news that the indian press today has seemed to forsake. here’s charting the other side of the coin. as in life, so in death. left, right & centre: was tata beloved by all? in a statement to its members on wednesday, following the barrage of digital news articles & political announcements marking tata’s demise as a tragic loss to the nation, leftist youth organisation collective’s delhi general secretary, sourya observed that the mournful camp in the event of tata's death had seemingly united people from diametric ends of the political spectrum. “today, the 'leftist' chief minister of kerala and a billionaire from gujarat are both paying tribute to ratan tata. it is a matter of great pride for any individual when ideological opponents come together in mourning, but this reflects something deeper,” it opens. “today, the 'leftist' chief minister of kerala and a billionaire from gujarat are both paying tribute to ratan tata. it is a matter of great pride for any individual when ideological opponents come together in mourning, but this reflects something deeper.” sourya, general secretary, collective delhi this is in reference to tweets 5 by cpi(m)’s pinarayi vijayan and businessman gautam adani respectively. vijayan was elected kerala's chief minister as well as the leader of the left democratic front back in 2016 6 , two positions he has held since, & is among the country’s most prominent of leftist voices. gautam adani, on the other hand, is the most powerful name backing the indian right wing at time of writing, whose rise to becoming the second richest man in india parallelled incumbent prime minister narendra modi’s political rise from a controversial gujarati cm struggling with a pr crisis to being elected leader of the executive for three consecutive terms after he extended financial support to him in the aftermath of the godhrā kānd 7 . indeed, the two could not be further apart in terms of what they represent to the ideological indian, & yet both seem to have come together in writing x (formerly twitter) eulogies for tata. this dichotomy, between right, left & tata, is not an isolated & interesting case study of human multitudes, but something that has remained ever-present throughout the partly fabled tale of the tata group’s 200-year 8 tumultuous history. tata’s institutions & architectures have long defined the murky space of the indian political centre, having been founded as a business empire that formed the very blueprint of industry in a mixed economy. as india’s economy has shifted away from the part-socialist model to an increasingly capitalist one, the conglomerate’s constitution has similarly evolved. yet even in 2024, in the steel rods that hold up this country & in the military vehicles that surveil it, the dichotomy survives. bastar, tata steel, & the ‘biggest land grab since columbus’ while adani’s posthumous reverence of tata has been called out by veteran journalist ravish kumar & popular consensus 9 permissions, and strictly individualised. so it is unsurprising that as the conversations begin to drag on, and as the sans-mic stage is slowly and quietly wrestled away from the protesters that initiated, organised, and made up the majority of the protest to those that prevented it from happening in front of my eyes, that the tension gets stronger. the speeches begin to meld together, and the testimonies turn into rants. a woman from the rwa group turns to the circle and implores all women to hold men accountable at all stages of violence, directly addressing the domestic workers. thing. “you have to stop them at the first step. when someone touches you in the bus, publicly shame him! i have done it. i did when i was in my 20s! it discourages them from doing more.” a few more responsibility is not all ours. i wonder if the conversation has moved forward a single step from where anita’s speech left off, and don’t bother wondering too hard. i stop recording the speeches and start taking notes on who speaks and for how long. a total of 15 speeches are delivered by the end of the hour, not counting cross-conversation – only four by domestic workers, and not one of them uninterrupted. when a woman standing beside anita tries to discuss how this protest is a good start, but we need to keep up this momentum when the same thing happens to a daughter from a poor household like hers, the b2 block women standing opposite her plead to the group that no, “it’s about all women. all of our daughters deserve to be safe.” fifteen minutes later when the same thing is said by a woman in jeans and a short kurti, citing the rape of a 6-year-old in up , the group bursts with applause. it’s a terrible thing to say, but i’m bored. when the discussion isn’t infuriating, it’s shameful. in a conversation over tea & bidis a few days later, collective delhi’s head and phd scholar sourya would tell me, “if anything, the conversation has gone backward from where it was during nirbhaya. institutional policy was upfront, and the critique of rape culture was a lot more scathing.” the speeches at the protest seem intent on illustrating his point. two women beside me are having a sidebar, one of whom is named rehaya. as yet another rwa woman goes on about shaming eve teasers as a rape-preventing strategy, i join in. from the centre of the semicircle, a domestic worker who has been vocal from the start shares an incident where she and her family beat up a guy harassing their daughter on their street. “ma’am, this happened to us once. we beat him up, we beat him up good,” she says. “very good, you did well.” the rwa members approve. rehaya, personally, does not share my derision - of course, according to shreya & arundhati, neither do the majority of the union or its activists - or that of the women around who are planning their escapes. her only contention is that for all the talk of all women standing for all others, all women hardly stand against all men. “these boys are also someone’s sons, aren’t they? when their sons do something, do they support the girl? of course not, they don’t even believe her. they think their sons can do no wrong.” someone from the other end says that violence isn’t the answer. and so it goes. 9:45 | dispersal another 15 minutes of talking later, shreya asks us all to hold hands and form a chain. the clusters appear again, divided cleanly by kho-kho poles of people holding posters standing in between, such that no one has to touch anyone they don’t want to. a few days later when i tell shreya about this story to try to score some interviews she is less than elated. she shares with me her apprehensions about comparing a comfortable inter-class protest with an incident as ‘extreme’ as hiranandani’s, which are understandable. i explain to her that the comparison is not one of degree, but of foundation, which helps but does not satisfy her. she defends the b2 residents with all her might. “they were only speaking because we asked them to speak. what happened here was completely different. some of the b2 women even held hands with their maids,” she says, like it helps her case. “the women mathematics even exists. i appreciated this insight, as it revealed to me the ways propaganda and revisionist history are not found only in the mathematics context of the usa, but are universal. i also appreciated learning about the controversy over the ways that mathematics in india is situated and talked about. and i especially appreciated the connection back to the unjust caste system, particularly because it reinforced the little that i knew about the ways that brahmin ideology often positions itself as the one and only true caste, and thereby the official holders of mathematics knowledge.” - theodore chao , professor of mathematics, ohio state university. second, professor subramanian brought up that professor arora did not mention that the idea of vedic mathematics actually subramanian brought this up. for a conference like icme, i feel we should be talking heavily about humanity and injustice, particularly within mathematics education. so this information helped me situate and understand culturally the role and space of what is labeled as vedic mathematics. third, professor subramanian mentioned that some of the books and articles that were cited about vedic mathematics in the introduction had been discredited. professor subramanian even mentioned that one of the cited authors had disavowed the idea that a 'vedic' mathematics even exists. i appreciated little that i knew about the ways that brahmin ideology often positions itself as the one and only true caste, and thereby the official holders of mathematics knowledge,” wrote chao. for this, she was
