been part of for its past three iterations, having chaired a study group herself in the previous one. according to a report by the federal, which has since been deleted, ‘security guards escorted 101: theodore chao’s testimony of professor jayasree subramanian’s actions in the session “reviving ancient wisdom: vedic mathematics for modern learning” facilitated by ashish arora this testimony was written in defense of professor jayasree subramanian, who was expelled from the recently held 15th icme in sydney due to the incident described above. chao’s testimony has been widely circulated through academic circles, & is largely responsible for shedding light on the controversy. my name is theodore chao and i am a professor of mathematics education at the ohio state university. i am honored to be an invited speaker at the international congress of mathematics education (icme) conference in sydney, australia in 2024. this is my second icme conference and i came because i love hearing and discussing global perspectives of mathematics education and learning to eradicate past injustices. yesterday, july 12, i attended a 9:00 am session titled, 'reviving ancient wisdom: vedic mathematics for modern learning', facilitated by professor ashish arora of i. k. gujral punjab technical university. i attended the session because i was interested in cultural ways of thinking about mathematics and mathematics teaching practices, particularly ones that come from non-eurocentric backgrounds. my limited understanding of indian mathematics history made me curious to attend this session and i did so with an open mind, without assumptions that there might be issues of injustice and oppression within what would be presented as vedic mathematics. personally, i found the session to be quite disappointing, but not terrible. professor arora only briefly spoke about the origins of vedic mathematics and the different mathematicians who were considered vedic mathematicians in india. i wish he had spent more time on speaking about and engaging us in discussion about the cultural history of mathematics, as this was supposed to be a workshop session. but he quickly glossed through this history in about 15 or 20 minutes. then, professor arora introduced various mathematics procedures framed as particular aspects of vedic mathematics. i would have found these procedures fascinating if we had time to unpack them, play with them, and discuss their histories. instead, professor arora jumped into examples and specific details about the way to use these procedures in isolated ways, unconnected to real-world mathematics. i tried to follow along with various ways that he presented specific values within algorithms that would lead to multiplication. personally, i found these examples to be quite boring because professor arora seemed to be lecturing and just walking through the examples quickly without really interacting with the audience. in fact, i even intervened to move the whiteboard he was using to a space that was more well-lit and visible to the rest of the room to make this lecture a little more engaging to the audience. i was disappointed because it felt very much like a traditional (not in a good way) college mathematics lecture, one in which the professor did not seem interested in connecting with the audience or even listening to what the audience was thinking. this is an aspect of this workshop that i found frustrating. to me, the main point of the icme conference is to explore and discuss mathematics education together. therefore, having space to engage in the study of mathematics pedagogy and the ways that mathematics is connected to actual humans seems to be a necessary part of any content presented at this conference. during the lecture, i, as well as the woman sitting next to me, were having trouble following the mathematics that was being presented. we felt frustrated at the pace of the presentation. and we wondered if there were typos on the slides because we had trouble generating the same answers that were presented. professor arora did not seem to acknowledge this or want to engage the audience about our understanding. this was frustrating as i felt that a pause for discussion would have been pedagogically appropriate. about 45 minutes into the session (9:45 am), i heard one of the participants in the room ask if there would be room for discussion. the speaker answered that, yes, there would be time for discussion and just kept continuing lecturing. i noticed that me and the other participants around me all seemed disappointed that we did not start a discussion at that time. when there were 15 minutes left in this 1.5-hour session (10:15 am), professor arora opened up time for discussion. by this point, i had given up any attempt to follow along with the mathematics being presented. professor jayasree subramanian, who was sitting a row behind me, raised her hand and was called on. professor subramanian stood up and raised a few, well-organized points. first, professor subramanian raised the point that the presenter was presenting indian mathematics as one of only two mathematics cultures, european mathematics being the other. she questioned why professor arora did not acknowledge the other forms of mathematics such as chinese or egyptian or inca mathematics and mentioned that not acknowledging other mathematical cultures is problematic. second, professor subramanian brought up that professor arora did not mention that the idea of vedic mathematics actually centers the idea of brahmin supremacy within the unjust caste system that still pervades india today. personally, i did not know much about this background. so, i appreciated that professor subramanian brought this up. for a conference like icme, i feel we should be talking heavily about humanity and injustice, particularly within mathematics education. so this information helped me situate and understand culturally the role and space of what is labeled as vedic mathematics. third, professor subramanian mentioned that some of the books and articles that were cited about vedic mathematics in the introduction had been discredited. professor subramanian even mentioned that one the cited authors had disavowed the idea that a vedic mathematics even exists. i appreciated this insight, as it revealed to me the ways propaganda and revisionist history are not found only in the mathematics context of the usa, but are universal. i also appreciated learning about the controversy over the ways that mathematics in india is situated and talked about. and i especially appreciated the connection back to the unjust caste system, particularly because it reinforced the little that i knew about the ways that brahmin ideology often positions itself as the one and only true caste, and thereby the official holders of mathematics knowledge. to me, these comments were great ways to start a conversation. professor subramanian spoke loudly so that the whole room could hear her. and she spoke with passion. her comments seemed respectful and in line with opening up academic discourse. after this, another participant stood up to speak. this participant mentioned that there was a space to engage in a critical unpacking of vedic mathematics. but that, perhaps that critical conversation was not appropriate at this session. then, because it was now 10:30 am, the session was finished and we all walked outside. after the session was over, i saw professor subramanian outside and i thanked her for her comments. i felt that without her comments, i would've left this session frustrated because it felt very much like a mathematics lecture and not a mathematics education workshop. i also felt that there were a number of ideas that came up in the session that were glossed over quickly, such as the role of the vedic mathematicians, the connections of the vedic mathematics to real-world mathematics, or even the ways that these ideas connected to mathematics teaching or teacher education. without professor subramanian’s comments, i would've been frustrated and felt that i had spent an hour and a half in what was supposed to be a workshop and not really learned anything at all. but professor subramanian’s comments helped connect the content presented to the realm of mathematics education and helped me better understand the sociopolitical space of how vedic mathematics is situated. through professor subramanian’s comments, i learned that the term vedic is problematic, and that there are issues of power and caste and hierarchies deeply involved in this way of thinking about mathematics. this lens helped me better reflect on this session and the ways it connects to larger issues within our field of mathematics education globally. in no way did i find anything that professor subramaniam said to be antagonistic or confrontational. nor did i feel that there was any risk of violence or threats in the room. in fact, i felt that the conversations that came about because of jayasree’s comments led to a better conversation for everybody in the room because it helped connect the content to mathematics education. i have since learned that professor subramanian was expelled from the icme conference because of her comments in this session. to me, this decision feels unjust and unnecessarily harsh. from what i saw, professor subramanian was bringing up points to better connect this workshop to the goals of icme. without her comments, this would have been an inappropriate mathematics lecture that had no connection to icme. even though i am an invited speaker and member of the icme community, i ended up spending the rest of my saturday missing sessions of the conference that i would have liked to have attended and participated in because i learned about this injustice to professor subramanian. to me, it feels that professor subramanian is being unjustly targeted because she dared to call out injustice and the relationship of the indian caste system to the content of this session. i also note that professor subramanian is an indian woman who speaks with a strong and authoritative voice. positioning her as a threat seems to invoke the same forms of misogyny and racism that continually oppress women of color globally. this treatment of professor subramanian is unjust and unwarranted. this experience has made me question the decision-making ability of the icme conference organizers and wonder if this conference is a safe space for women of color. will the future of icme be a space that lauds white supremacy, misogyny, and elitism within mathematics education? i have no interest in being a part of that icme. theodore chao is an associate professor of mathematics education in the department of teaching and learning at the ohio state university. his research agenda involves engaging all students and teachers regardless of social identity (race, gender, socioeconomic status, etc.) to fully see themselves as mathematical humans, particularly through technology. chao is currently an associate editor for theory into practice (tip), an editorial panel member of mathematics teacher educator (mte), a steering committee member of the north american chapter of the international group for the psychology of mathematics education (pme-na), and an organizer for the free minds, free people (fmfp) conference.
100: post '67, pockets of palestine surrounded by israeli settlements have learnt to live with a strange & psychologically grotesque consequence of long-term military occupation: bored soldiers. 16th july 2024, new delhi : on october 22nd, 2023, a mere two weeks after october 7th, a video was posted to tiktok showing a man describing a visit to his sister's home in a small hebron village called beit ummar, & their life along the occupied west bank. he described a game the soldiers played with palestinian families in the area, explained to him by his own nephew and brother-in-law. it was a game of 'statue', as people who grew up in parts of the world not under active warfare would recall playing, where a group of runners freezes up in response to a commanding catcher, yelling out the preferred variant of the band of neighborhood rascals: ice! freeze! lock! tag! statue! in beit ummar, the command is not heard but seen, in the form of laser pointers from sniper rifles. and the soldiers always chase. "i visited my sister in her home in beit ummar, which is a village in hebron. sitting atop a hill their beautiful home was surrounded by three israeli settlements. i woke up in the middle of the night with my nephew & brother-in-law standing next to me - they'd spotted several laser pointers pointing into the house from one of the settlements that are nearby. and when i asked them what was happening, they told me to stay lying in bed because this is often a game that settlers played with them. the "game" was laser pointers from sniper rifles in the house at all times, so they knew that they could take a shot whenever they wanted." - @candide_freeman on tiktok, posted 22nd october 2023, with 5 likes & 1 share. journalist leila warah (@leila.shw on instagram) describes this phenomenon as a common, almost ordinary occurrence in areas like beit ummar, which are populated by native residents leftover after the six day war back in '67, outnumbered & surrounded by israeli settlements. an evolved form of settler violence, born less from malice or urgency, and - rather terrifyingly - more from boredom. areas with a larger displaced population - & consequently stronger military presence - on the other hand, like refugee camps & epicenters of post-october 7th attacks see their own versions of these 'second-person shooter games'. drones flying up to balconies & uttering eerily human threats in distinctly unhuman voices ("we are in wartime," says a drone to an elderly man while hovering outside his balcony. "we advise you to take caution. and take care of your kids. whoever thinks of doing something, we will get to him. we are in wartime…"), remote-controlled guns that seem to track movement; air-dropped aid that kills. in aida refugee camp, where leila warah lives & works, daily life looks very different from that in beit ummar. like most refugee camps, the overwhelming presence around aida is not that of settlers but of soldiers. the unrwa recognises 58 palestinian camps (not including 10 more formed after '67) across the occupied land, & even among them, aida is highly surveilled . at the entrance of this camp sits a remote-controlled gun. one that points at every passerby, & is triggered by untested artificial intelligence . "i've gone up to it to film a couple of times, but this is a relatively dangerous area," warah begins, elaborating on her personal encounters with the notorious firearm on al jazeera's the stream . "soldiers are bored. they're just maybe sitting there & they kinda want to mess with you. i've gone up there to film the remote-controlled gun - all i'm carrying is a camera - & i see the gun just kind of… twist & turn towards me, where it's pointed directly at me." she tells the story like she's told it a million times before. "soldiers are bored. they're just maybe sitting there & they kinda want to mess with you. you feel like a hamster sitting in a test wheel. they're just playing with you." - leila warah, ajstream on al jazeera, 16th july, 2024. she says it like it bores her. because of course, in a state that's been on lockdown for 75 years, it isn't just the soldiers who have nothing to do. in siri miri , a palestinian short film about youth & boredom in a 21st-century apartheid nation directed by luay awwad , a sniper rifle being pointed at two teenagers enjoying a bonfire is treated as little more than a joke, and one that's low-hanging fruit at that. the scene seems to jab at the casualty of the encounter, glossing over the drama of a near-death experience in favor of that of a torched friday night plan, as if the snipers are just mischievous old coots outside of the frame, teasing our boys as they skulk off in defeat. a cartoonish nemeses, with cartoonish gravity. the scene speaks to the peaceful global resident something so foreign they can do little more than scoff at the absurdity of it all; offering sympathy where it isn't needed, & will be unflinchingly rejected. 'feel sorry that the fucker ruined our bonfire again,' awwad says in his film. 'there's nothing else for you to feel sorry about.' what is interesting about siri miri is that contrary to popular understanding of freedoms & everyday life in palestine before october 7th, the film was released in 2021, long before netanyahu's military campaign in the region, & the degree of infrastructural control shown in it (water, movement, electricity, rations, safety) is far from the worst exercised by israel in the west bank, either in the past or in the present. "take care of your kids." - israeli drone outside palestinian family's balcony, @yumna.hp on tiktok, 3rd december 2023. there's a sadistic sense of humour with which the israeli military has come to operate in palestine, a humour that could only have evolved from a relationship of violence, control, & colonisation that has lasted half a century. a disturbing intimacy to the familiarity with which israeli soldiers point their guns at palestinians; a reverse stockholm syndrome between keeper & kept, as if the terror they cause is but a drawn-out abusive marriage they don't recognise themselves outside of. 'what do they mean they don't want to be tortured & killed? what do they mean they don't want to have their homes stolen & bombed? what do they mean they don't love my boot on their neck?' what do you mean you don't want to play? based on leila warah's interview aired alongside curated tiktok posts on the stream hosted by anelise borges on al jazeera (english) on 16th july 2024. report compiled by the voice express.

98: the petitioner behind the pil to remove arvind kejriwal from the post of delhi cm makes a unique hobby out of public interest litigations, and his legal portfolio paints quite the picture. new delhi, 30th march 2024: recently, a pil was filed before the delhi high court seeking the removal of arvind kejriwal from the post of chief minister of delhi in light of his arrest by the enforcement directorate in the liquor policy case. [surjit singh yadav v union of india and ors] . the plea was rejected by the delhi hc stating that it fell outside the scope of judicial interference. however, it brought attention to an avid petitioner surjit singh yadav who appears to have a long history of filing various and ridiculous public interest litigations in the past. who is surjit singh yadav? the president of ‘ hindu sena ’ (as per his linkedin profile), yadav is a self-proclaimed farmer and social worker who has been actively involved in filing pils that seek to address various legal matters, all of which follow a distinct pattern of weaponising the law to achieve frivolous ends in the name of addressing issues of public interest and accountability. in this legal profile, we delve into some of yadav's most prominent public interest litigations (pils). surjit singh yadav's organisation, the hindu sena, also has a long-standing history of run-ins with the law, of both violating and utilising it (see: hindu sena says it vandalised signboard outside us embassy, 1 arrested | delhi news - the indian express and hindu sena moves sc seeking action for hate speeches against sanatan dharma ). a pseudo-terrorist fringe group, it frequently invails the law and moves court to protect the sanctity of the hindu religion. much of yadav's petitionary concern mirrors this, illustrating his trivialisation of the judicial system as well as his recurring demands of it to advance his own personal political agendas. the kejriwal petition yadav’s recent pil sought to restrain chief minister arvind kejriwal from issuing orders while in police custody of the directorate of enforcement (ed) and also requested not to provide typist or computer facilities to kejriwal during this time. through advocates shashi ranjan kumar singh and mahesh kumar, the petitioner further stated that arvind kejriwal, while issuing directions and orders in custody, is breaching his oath of secrecy administered to him under the third schedule of the constitution of india. the pil appears to address concerns regarding governance and accountability in delhi's administration. yadav moved the court through a writ petition under article 226, requesting a quo warranto against kejriwal to clarify his authority as cm. he contended that the government of the national capital territory of delhi rules, 1993, empowers the cm to request files from any department, and highlighted that if kejriwal remains cm, he could demand investigations into files where he is implicated. the plea was rejected by the high court. a division bench of acting chief justice manmohan and justice manmeet pritam singh arora said: “having heard the counsel for the petitioner and having perused the paper-book, this court is of the view that there is no scope for judicial interference in the present matter. this court in writ jurisdiction cannot remove or dismiss respondent no. 4 (kejriwal) from the post of chief minister of the government of nct of delhi or declare breakdown of constitutional machinery in the state. it is for the other organs of the state to examine the said aspect in accordance with law.” but what’s interesting is this is not the first time that a court has had to explain the jurisdiction of the judiciary to mr. yadav, and it likely won’t be the last. (update, 1st april 2024: the very next day after this article was written, another petition by yadav was presented in the delhi high court). how many pils has surjit singh yadav filed? though the petition led to little consequence other than bringing yadav's name back to media attention, it is noteworthy that this is not the first pil he has filed, or second, (or third). as per judicial records between 2022 and 2024, yadav has filed at least six (update, 1st april 2024: now seven) pils in two years, and three in the past two weeks alone, on march 20th, 28th, and the 1st of april. all three of these petitions, filed after the enforcement of the code of conduct , have raised allegations against political parties; notably opposition parties to the current bjp-led government. all of yadav’s petitions have been presented in higher courts and dismissed, either on grounds of baselessness and irrelevance or withdrawn in response to questioning. (edit, 1st april 2024: as of one day after the writing of this article, this is no longer true. yadav’s second petition for the dismissal of kejriwal has been forwarded to the special district court that will hear the ed’s case against the cm before being disposed of.) this article will detail two of these three recent pils, along with another controversial one from last year. why does it matter that they are ‘pil’s? it is important to note here that filing a pil is not quite the same as filing any other ordinary lawsuit. as the delhi high court reminded yadav’s counsel during the hearing of his first pil hearing this year - “the courts exercising their power of judicial review found to their dismay that the poorest of the poor, the depraved (sic), the illiterate, the urban and rural unorganized labour sector, women, children, those handicapped by "ignorance, indigence and illiteracy and other downtrodden persons have either no access to justice or had been denied justice. a new branch of proceedings known as "social action litigation" or "public interest litigation" was evolved with a view to render complete justice to the aforementioned classes of persons. it expanded its wings in course of time. the courts in pro bono publico granted relief to inmates of prisons, provided legal aid, directed speedy trials, maintenance of human dignity and covered several other areas.” ( supreme court in guruvayoor devaswom managing committee and anr. vs. c.k. rajan and ors. , (2003) 7 scc 546) courts not only bear the cost of pil’s but fast track them, prioritising them over other cases clogging india’s judicial system, relaxing legal restrictions, & hearing them directly in high courts & the supreme court, because this is the only way that the downtrodden in our society can receive justice. among the many matters that surjit singh yadav has been habitually making use of this tool of social justice for, have been cases defending corporations & industrialists alleged to have received loan waivers from the central government, questioning whether the taj mahal was really built by the mughals, & trying to prevent an arrested politician from accessing stationary. the following sections expand on each of these cases in further detail. the taj mahal story in november 2023, a plea put forth by surjit singh yadav asserted that the 17th-century monument, taj mahal, was originally the residence of raja man singh, later refurbished by the mughal emperor shah jahan. the court observed that mr. yadav had previously submitted a similar plea to the supreme court, which was withdrawn after he suggested providing a representation to the asi back in december 2022. in his plea, first called to hearing in the supreme court in november 2022, yadav had claimed that as per his research, a mansion already existed at the site where the taj mahal is built. and argued that the apparent absence of a named architect for the mausoleum in historic documents ‘quite clearly indicates that the mansion of raja man singh was not demolished but only modified and renovated to create the current look of the taj mahal.’ "he has certainly brought out many historical facts that are very interesting." additional solicitor general (asg) chetan sharma stated, appearing for the center. the apex court declined to consider the plea, emphasising that pils should not be used for speculative inquiries and that courts are not in place to revisit historical matters, & clearly concluded the matter with, “no further adjournment shall be granted on any ground.” yadav then sought permission to withdraw his plea and make a representation before the archaeological survey of india, which was granted in december. (case title: surjt singh yadav v. uoi and ors.) yadav looked for explicit mandates from the archeological survey of india (asi), the focal government, the public files of india, and the uttar pradesh government. in his request, yadav claimed that he has led broad exploration of the taj mahal and demanded the expulsion of ‘verifiable errors’ concerning the development of the taj mahal from reading material and asked the asi to lead an examination concerning the age of the construction and the presence of raja man singh's royal residence. he also contended that different books about the taj mahal contain clashing data, for example, one book recommending that shah jahan's better half was aliya begum without any notice of mumtaz mahal. but it didn’t end there. yadav filed another petition next year in november 2023, after making this representation to asi, this time in the delhi high court, despite having received no validating response from the research organisation, & receiving clear instruction from the supreme court regarding the scope of judicial interference (or lack thereof). the petition was dismissed immediately. “4. learned asg has fairly stated before this court once a representation is preferred, the archaeological survey of india will look into it. 5. in the light of aforesaid, no further orders are required to be passed in the present pil as the petitioner has already submitted a representation in the matter. the same stands disposed of accordingly.” (surjit singh yadav vs union of india and ors on 3 november 2023) the curious case of corporate concern on 20th march 2024, another recent pil filed by surjit singh yadav aimed to initiate an investigation and legal action against congress leader rahul gandhi, delhi chief minister arvind kejriwal and president of samajwadi party, akhilesh yadav. the crux of the allegation is that the individuals have purportedly made misleading or false statements regarding the waiver of loans for industrialists, thus tarnishing the reputation of the central government as well as the nation. the high court, however, stated that the industrialists and the individuals who are alleged to have been defamed had the means and resources to approach the court and file appropriate proceedings, by themselves. during the hearing, acting chief justice manmohan told yadav's counsel: “if people or industrialists are aggrieved, they will take action. how can we interfere in this? don't underestimate the wisdom of voters. don't speak their mind, please. don't involve us in this….” “someone misleads, someone leads. let the people take the call. don't get us involved in this. if people are aggrieved, they will take action. why should we relax the principle of locus standi to entertain the pil?” furthermore, the pil sought directives concerning political parties such as the indian national congress, aam aadmi party, and samajwadi party, as well as media outlets news 24, x (formerly twitter), and youtube, to remove the purportedly false and misleading statements from their respective platforms. yadav argued that the statements were disseminated with the intention to create confusion among readers or viewers, thereby aiming to undermine the image of the central government. “this court is also of the view that the principle of relaxation of locus standi is not called for in this petition. the petitioner underestimates the wisdom of the indian voters. accordingly, this court is of the view that no orders are called in the writ petition and the same is closed,” the high court said. ( delhi hc rejects plea seeking action against rahul, kejriwal, akhilesh for ‘false’ statements - the hindu ) a joke of justice while it would be a lot funnier to approach this story as one of human interest & oddity, the truth is surjit’s affinity for the pil is not an individualistic quirk or just an interesting choice of hobby. the hindu sena, literally translating to ‘hindu army’ is not just a fringe religious group that’s part & parcel of a free society. since its inception in 2011, the ‘ngo’ has taken credit for acts of mass beatings, vandalism of public & private property, & if it rings a bell, held a havan for donald trump because he would ‘defeat islam.’ the hindu sena is a radical fascist organisation that has displayed its capacity for violence over & over again, & the only reason it has not yet gotten classified as a terrorist front is that it bears the flag of the wrong religion. surjit’s case is not a unique one. the advocate responsible for presenting all of his petitions is the same one who presented vishnu gupta’s - the other name publicly listed as president & founder of hindu sena. in march 2022, gupta, filed a pil highlighting concerns regarding the offers and promises - now colloquially referred to as ‘freebies’ - made by political parties in the ongoing assembly elections, which the court rejected due to targeting specific political parties instead of having genuine reform suggestions. “ you have a hidden agenda. who are you?" asked the court. “i am a devotee.” replied his counsel. so it goes. it seems, that beyond physical violence, organisations like the hindu sena & the individuals that make them have turned the pil into a weapon, corrupting a tool of social justice into one that wastes resources & time, distracts the nation from pre-existing problems by creating new ones that didn’t need solving, & in this sense inflicts far greater damage to india’s democracy than any physical attack could manage; it seeks to weaken our judicial machinery, laughable case after laughable case. and the tragedy, is the courts seem to have no intention to penalise them. in a judicial system that views acts as minor as drinking water in courtrooms as contempt, it needs to be asked why a repeated violation of pil principles by people like surjit singh yadav & vishnu gupta is never met with anything more than oral chidings. (edit, 10th april 2024: the delhi high court has imposed a fine of rs. 50,000 on sandeep kumar after receiving what is the third petition in 10 days on the subject of dismissing kejriwal, which is at least a slap on the wrist, but still short of legal accountability) are judges only offended when a woman wears short sleeves on the stand? is it not in ‘contempt of the court’ to not once, not twice, but repeatedly disregard judicial direction & make, in the words of acting chief justice of the delhi hc, a mockery out of the system? (see: delhi hc dismisses third plea for arvind kejriwal's removal from cm post, says costs only way to curb such pleas - dynamite news ) evidently not. perhaps it never was. chronology of surjit singh yadav’s petitions 2nd march 2022: diary 6179/2022 3rd march 2022: diary 6179/2022 28th november 2022: diary 28636/2022 5th december 2022: diary 28636/2022 10th may 2023: diary 6090/2023 6th september 2023: diary 6090/2023 3rd november 2023: diary 14336/2023 20th march 2024: diary 4218/2024 28th march 2024: diary 4578/2024 1st april 2024: diary 4642/2024 based on a report by jia ahuja for the voice express.

96: as communal violence & bigotry scorched through the streets of delhi during the last caa protests, a quiet, unsuspecting documentary on a bird hospital ended up saying that on the subject of muslims & vermin which most immigration laws are afraid to. as the 2024 lok sabha elections loom closer, the bjp-led government has felt neither guilt nor shame in bringing back the caa into conversation & legislation. so it is only fair, that we also bring back to those who have (& introduce to those who haven't) experienced the masterpiece that was all that breathes . a snail moves on a windowsill as a fire burns on the street outside. all that breathes, 2022, shaunak sen. title: all that breathes genre: documentary duration: 97 minutes release: 2022 directed by: shaunak sen synopsis: as delhi’s air worsens for non-vegetarian birds and religions alike, three men attempt to save what they can among all that breathes. a close-up of a kite, all that breathes, 2022, shaunak sen. “we came to animals and science through our late mom’s fables about ghosts and holy spirits. the ‘cat-saint’, ‘vulture shrine’, spirits that appeared as snakes and insects. one shouldn’t differentiate between all that breathes.” all that breathes, 2022 a small frog stares into the distance, all that breathes, 2022, shaunak sen. saud and nadeem, two brothers running a veterinary hospital for birds of prey out of the basement of their brick laden west delhi family home along with their friend salik navigate the fiscal and familial difficulties of ‘saving kites’ as the family business as more and more birds fall from the sky in delhi’s worsening air, while a threat that has little to do with brotherhood or medicine begs whether they should be saving themselves instead. similar in structural principle to eeb allay ooo! (2019, prateek vats), all that breathes alternates from exquisite and beautiful shots of the city and its wildlife to the unpretentious, voyeuristic comedy of a middle class delhi man's everyday. the transitions and fills are lingering and gorgeous, making the most judicious and clever use of narration possible, collaging painstakingly personal, breathtaking moments of breath itself within the city with insights from two self made veterans of the same. centipede breaking the surface of a puddle as an aeroplane flies overhead. rats having a pixar dinner by a burst-gutter sein. cows migrating across a storm clogged river. flies on a car deck. everything that breathes. not a moment is wasted, not a single set half assed. the sound is withheld and haunting, it tells with what it doesn't tell. the backdrop of the streets screams with protests and political agitation as salik opens a refrigerator filled with meat. news headlines of the progression of violence over the caa score the outline of themselves overlayed on shots of the streets and people. the whole film walks a circle around this violence; around prejudice and words. only one section within the entire film even bothers stating violence, explicitly - not in as many words, but in pictures, and those too not of the violence itself, but of it's aftermath. of the space left behind by it, of the ashes left in its wake. it lasts for less than a minute. it is silent. "by calling people termites and rats, they've somehow made it about hygiene. just like the kite's different, people are also treated differently. violence is always an act of communication." all that breathes , 2022 rats scurry over a trash covered streetside in delhi, all that breathes, 2022, shaunak sen there is a term, for cinematic behaviour like this. environmental storytelling. telling a story not with what is there but with what is around it. "what's a crater?" "a hole where something happened." room , 2010, emma donaghue every single one of the film's 97 minutes is hand sculpted around this principle. ultimately, all that breathes is a film that chooses to be about the smaller picture. cutout of empty space on the road, "what is a streetlight?" a streetlight is what is not there. it rejects the opportunity to say what it therefore ends up saying much more clearly; it is as much about nadeem and saud and what is left unsaid between them as the political commentary that it will end up being remembered for (one that it perhaps only makes incidentally). it is as much about the cost of doing something noble as it is about something noble perhaps not being enough. it is as much about the critters writhing in the dirt stuck underneath our fingernails as those blacklisted in the citizenship amendment act. sometimes, all a parent can leave his child behind with is purpose. perception can be a lineage, too, you know. all that breathes is as much about why some men do what they do as it is about recognising that there is no reason for them to want to, any more than you and me. it dares you to recontinue the convenience of transferring the burden of care onto those who have the spine to carry it under the guise of acknowledging the goodness of their hearts. of your miserable attempts to justify your apathy, your inaction, your gutlessness. it dares you to look a black kite in the eye from an inch away and not fall in love with it because it kills to eat. this is the worth of technical excellence; no labour of love is invisible. this film falls to me, within the unnervingly small category of perfect; deeply funny, deeply human, and absolutely flawless. it dares you to decide or admit that you've already decided - what is too dirty for you to mourn? anomalous, but precisely because it isn’t; following along a disturbing pattern of mismanagement at an institute that, despite its a+ naac accreditation, is plagued by a lack of seriousness. this article was pitched by shruti patel. head of design at tve, shruti is a beginner in the design field. she likes to work with illustrations, ux design and packaging, & (this part is not written by her) her eye is incomperable. she also writes sometimes. conflict of interest statement: this article is about kalindi college, delhi university, which is where tve was founded in 2022.
93: manoj jangra, a small business owner in new delhi’s dwarka, & a crpf retiree tells us why he likes modi, & you should too. hidden away in a basement in one of the many residential streets turned markets of south-west delhi, is a photo framing shop run by a crpf retiree & his homemaker-turned-craftswoman wife. they have three children & a nephew; ms. jangra’s younger brother lives in the city with his wife & son, & quit his company job with terrible hours & terrible pay to work at the shop. it’s a family business. paintings & bulk posters bought wholesale from sadar bazaar line the walls of the shop; ram vivah pose a, ram vivah pose b, shiv vivah (a rarity), lakshmi ganesh sitting pose (‘seated gods are good luck’). along with online orders of album posters & lyric art, the things that sell the most at their shop are gods. mr. jangra opened this shop back in 2014, after becoming disillusioned with the government institutions he was working for during the lokpal protests. if you ask him why he quit his job at the crpf, he has a very clear answer. “because of kejriwal,” he says. “at the time there was congress at the center, & the corruption was suffocating. there was no end to it. i wasn’t even working for the government anymore, i was just working for individuals, all of them corrupt. kejriwal used to speak so well. he fought the government fearlessly. he was so bold, he said he would pass the lokpal bill, end the disparity. that these officers won’t travel as vips anymore. they will be like us. i was very moved by his promises. i fell for them.” today, thirteen years after the people of india took to the streets to fight congress’ rule of corruption, the lokpal protests remain a testament to the power of public dissent. the roar of a nation, following the voice of a small, insignificant man. arvind kejriwal’s words were powerful enough to move manoj jangra to reject a life of civil service, security, & a salary. the epic photo frames of today is a product of blood, sweat & tears, literally, as one finds out the hard way when one sets up a photo framing business from scratch. mr. jangra taught his wife & brother in law all they know today, but ten years ago, he had to teach himself. today though, manoj jangra has lost faith in kejriwal. if you ask him why, he says it is because kejriwal favors ‘one side more than the other.’ he thinks the aap government appeases the poor, & neglects the middle class. he is too much on the side of the destitute, at the cost of those who aren’t. today, epic photo frames is a well-respected & successful business, with regular patronage & a business network built upon trust & good practice, & manoj jangra is a well-respected man. he is everything that the indian middle class strives to be; strong-willed, self-made, & opinionated. but the politician of his favor today is no longer the aam aadmi , but the god . the foremost frames upon entering his store are 2x3 sq. ft wall hangings of ram lalla, & the sticker on top of his storefront reads ‘bjp ka parivaar.’ pros & cons: ‘achchhaiyan bhi toh ginwao.’ when business is slow & photoshop tutorials begin to bore him, mr. jangra likes to spend his time on politics. he is a frequent viewer of political commentary youtubers like mr. munnabhai, the jaipur dialogues, nitin shukla, the sham sharma show, & many more. though he describes himself as strongly right-leaning, such youtubers aren’t all he is content to see. he is a curious man, a fastidious believer in critical thinking & finding things out for yourself. one of his favourite creators is a pakistani youtuber named sohaib chaudhry, who runs the channel real entertainment tv focusing on socio-economic & cultural exchange between india & pakistan. he used to watch dhruv rathee, but doesn’t anymore. “ bohot hi negative way me lejata hai cheezon ko. har cheez mei burai. kabhi achhaia bhi toh ginwao.” (“he is too negative about everything. always recounting criticisms. one should take into account positives too.”) mr. jangra does not believe it is reasonable to be so robustly critical of a government, regardless of elections, timing, & party promises. he is in fact afraid, that if the party currently in power should lose, whatever good is being done (little or not) will be lost. if you ask him to reiterate why he doesn’t like kejriwal’s work in new delhi, though, he recounts the things that dissatisfy him. " road dekho. bahar bahar ke nahi, bahar bahar ke toh theek kara dete hai, kyunki whaan se toh ye netaon vagehra ki gaadiyan jayengi. yahan jahan aam janta rehta hai, kitne kharaab kar rakhe hai. meri scooty raise hi tooti this. ab gareeb aadmi ko farak nahi padta, road kaisa ho. toh ye kuchh nahi karte ." (“look at the roads. not the main ones, of course, the main ones are all fixed up, that’s where the ministers & the big men drive. but the ones here where ordinary men like me live, the roads are terrible. my scooty broke because of roads like these. but the poor don’t care about roads. so they do nothing.”) on being asked to elaborate on what some examples of the purported good that the central government has done may be, though, his eyes light up. contrary to what now under arrest delhi chief minister arvind kejriwal observed in his 2019 interview with kunal kamra, bjp supporters like manoj jangra do have an answer to the question (of just why it is that they like mr. narendra quite so much), & they have thought about it plenty. what, over the past 10 years, should we be grateful for? “ji pehli cheez toh hai security. aaj se 10 saal pehle dilli mei har jagah, buson mei, metro mei, sab jagah, announcement hote rehte the. ‘kisi anjaan vastu ko na chhuye isme bum ho sakta hai.’aaj kal sunai deti hai kahin?” (“the first thing is security. 10 years ago you could hear announcements in delhi, in the buses, metros, everywhere: ‘don't touch unidentified objects, they may contain bombs.’ do you hear them nowadays?”) perhaps the answer to that question is no, we do not, because despite the familiar bomb warning: “any unattended or suspicious articles like briefcase, bag, toy, thermos or transistor, etc could be a bomb,” being played on the delhi metro repeatedly, mr. jangra is confident that this is absolutely not the case. upon being asked whether he has attempted to verify this information or his hypothesis about them, mr. jangra is annoyed. “isme check karne ka kya hai? maine khud dekha hai apni aankhon se.” (“what is there to check? i've seen it with my own eyes.”) confident observations like these are what form the basis of much of the politics of mr. jangra, as well as that of most ordinary indians. this striking affinity for reason, logic, & critical thinking is characteristic of the right wing indian - he does not believe in books, facts, or numbers. he believes only in what can be understood with logic. he believes only in his own observations, which he also believes he arrives at independently. after all, there is no evidence more damning than an eyewitness testimony. in 2019, upon receiving complaints about the oversaturation of announcements on the magenta line, the dmrc announced that it would do away with 25 unessential announcements, & only 7 important ones would stay in place inside the trains. ‘security’ announcements like bomb alerts are the first of these seven. but that is neither logic nor reason. speaking of reason, one might observe (as is highly encouraged) that a decrease in safety announcements is not necessarily or sufficiently implicative of an increase in safety . but one would be wrong. upon asking mr. jangra why he thinks his observation implies or evidences his theory, he is again, annoyed. he does not like it when people refuse to use their own minds. he is not interested in proving to anyone what he thinks is obvious. “mai khud soch nahi sakta kya? ” (“can't i figure it out on my own?”) he can. and he is welcome to. upon analysis of terrorism databases & reports by tve it was found that there is indeed a correlation between terror attacks carried out before 2014 & after, just not the one mr. jangra suggests. on the contrary, the top five years in indian history by number of terrorist incidents, are all from the modi regime. but then again, correlation is not causation. and what credibility does the global terrorist database have, anyway, compared to an ex-crpf officer (retd. 2014) & a man with three generations' worth of relatives all over india & the world? when these statistics are quoted to him, he laughs in incredulity, finding them ridiculous. “you people will believe anything.” another of the modi government’s achievements that makes mr. jangra’s chest swell up with pride is the great strides india has made under its tenure in matters of military self-reliance. “ aaj se das saal pehle tak har cheez import hoti thi. har hathiyaar. koi bhi hathiyaar india mei nahi bante the. aaj dekh lo. haan jets vagehra toh import karne padte hi hai.” (“10 years ago everything used to be imported, every weapon. no weapon was made in india. look at us now. of course, we still have to import things like jets.”) this hindustan times article from 2012 illustrates just how abysmal india’s position in global arms trade was before the modi government came to power. today, not only are our import rates lower, but our export rates are higher than ever. much of this can be accredited to the strategic bans placed on imports of defense items over the last two years, which have now had four iterations. there has been an active push toward indigenisation, spearheaded by defence minister rajnath singh, & it has not come without cost. domestic procurement alone in the military budget progressively increased from ₹51,000 crores in 2020 to nearly twice that at ₹1 lakh crores in 2023 . in contrast, the entire allocation for education in the same budget was ₹1.2 lakh crores. this colossal jump in expenses is justified as being a temporary measure that will change india’s military dependence & make room for self-reliance, but 12 years & 12 progressively increasing budgets later, we are still the world’s largest importer of arms. we still don’t feature in even the top 25 arms-exporting nations. india’s import rates have gone down from 13% to 9.8%, a 3.2% decrease over 12 years, i.e. just 0.26% a year. the decrease of our reliance on russia has been parallelly accompanied by an increase of that on the west. but one must not always be critical. “ women’s safety dekh lo. buson mei aurton ke liye free ticketein. transport. bijli paani ki suvidhaayein. bohot kuch badla hai. bohot kuch behtar hua hai. jab mai dilli aaya tha toh hamara sir ke upar bulb tak nahi hota tha. ham andhere mei rehte the.” (“look at women's safety. there's free tickets for women in city buses. transport, water & electricity facilities. much has changed. much has improved. when i came to delhi we didn't even have a lightbulb above our heads. we used to live in the darkness.”) notably, free tickets for women in buses, free water & electricity for residential consumption, & last mile connectivity are all initiatives of the aam aadmi party-run delhi government, that have been taken, incidentally, also in the last 10 years. when reminded that transport, electricity, & water are jurisdictions of the state government, mr. jangra clarifies that he is speaking of improvements made to the nation at large. all of which, at the end of the day, are being made at the helm of the leader of the country: the prime minister. “ab dekho, apna ghar mai chalata hun. mere ghar mei kuch bhi achha hoga, meri beti tournament jeetegi ya mera beta afsar banega, toh ye meri bhi achievement hogi. desh pradhaan mantri chalata hai.” (“look, i run my house. an achievement in my house - say, my daughter wins a tournament or my son becomes an officer - is my achievement too. the prime minister runs the country.”) moving on from the impasse, mr. jangra began to conclude his argument. but a push for military self-reliance, a questionable idea of security, & the pmuy (pradhan mantri ujjwala yojana) scheme are far from the only ones on the long list of initiatives taken by the bjp-led central government over the past ten years that the average middle-class man rooting for narendra modi can recount. they must be. when asked to go on listing examples, mr. jangra promises to think & find more when he has the time. he hadn’t prepared for a presentation, after all. in the conversation that follows, the mood is nudged away from the intense & political to lighthearted small talk & chit chat. now that the procedural part of the interview is over, our correspondent offers commentary of their own on all that’s changed for the better in the modi regime. a upi payment card on the table can be seen standing out on the table, bright with colors of the indian flag; bharat interface for money. interestingly, india’s one-of-a-kind upi system is not a matter of pride to mr. jangra. he hardly even believes that western nations & china did not invent the technology first. “ haan par america ke paas toh aur pehle se tha, ” (“but america had the tech even earlier.”) he says, unsure, before our correspondent explains that he is confusing e-commerce technology with upi, a payments interface developed by the national payments corporation of india (npci). he laughs, embarrassed, explaining that he is not very well-versed in these things. he doesn’t even have paytm on his phone & prefers to use cash; the qr codes in his shop are a necessity of the trade. but he accepts our correspondent's praise for the technology with an open mind nevertheless. “i personally depend quite a bit on upi. a lot of people i know do. it is absurdly convenient,” she starts. “it is strange to think that for all matters that india is supposed to be behind so called ‘developed nations,’ a man who has lived here & is used to paytm, gpay, & the likes being the norm, will feel nothing but downgraded to move to say, a country like the us, that hasn’t yet figured out anything even close. as a matter of fact, there are talks of international collaboration in progress right now, including with the us itself. upi is a resource that india has built upon, that proves that time & money spent on infrastructural development still count for leverage in current world politics. new-age banking systems like the imps & upi are what india has to export.” she does not mention that the npci itself was established back in 2008, & its ownership has since been shared between several promoter banks, mostly private ones, & that narendra modi neither funded, initiated, nor endorsed the efforts behind making upi a success, as he did later on & with rupay. mr. jangra smiles at the monologue, happy to see that his encouragement to look at the bright side stuck. “fir log kehte hai vikaas nahi hota.” (“and then people say there isn't development.”) ' achhaiyan bhi toh ginwao' is a new irregular tve ground report series started in response to your feedback. in an attempt to meet the audience halfway with their reluctance to engage with media that is 'overly' critical of the powers that be, achaiyan bhi toh ginwao will attempt to, wherever possible, take a glass half full approach with reporting, but what it will also do & perhpas more importantly so, is dissect this desire for positive reportage itself.
92: amid media coverage of the 2024 farmer’s protests lending little sympathy to agricultural workers from delhi bordering states marching to the national capital, & plenty to the government using militant & violent means to suppress them, civilian apathy is profound. this is part one of a report on the public perception of the protest, & speculation over why it is what it is. 16th february 2024, new delhi: the 2024 farmer's protests come as an outcry against the central government's ignorance & apathy of the nation’s agricultural workers’ issues, with their prime concern being the continued refusal to ensure an msp to indian farmers as was guaranteed in both their 2014 & 2019 manifestos. in anticipation of unrest similar to the last iteration of these protests back in 2021 (wherein as well farmers from delhi bordering states marched to the national capital in response to three then-recent legislations), the government has taken to an aggressive obstruction of delhi borders. but with blockades & armed personnel keeping protesting farmers out of their capital, & internet shutdowns targeting protest centres, the steps taken by the bjp-led government have quickly become less about crowd control & more about shutting down the display completely. measures that were implemented in the hopes of preventing a violent escalation of conflict like last time have immediately turned violent themselves (read: police fire water cannons at farmers, used aerial drones to deploy teargas). when the talks on thursday, like the previous two rounds (on 8th & 12th february), remained inconclusive, farmers again abandoned what was a truce they’d temporarily agreed to for the discussion & stormed the shambhu border, leading to the infamous clash at the haryana-punjab border, where police & paramilitary forces fired tear gas shells & rubber bullets at the crowd for the third time. this was not a regrettable result of sudden & increased agitation, but a planned & repetitive intimidation strategy, as social media accounts of the march’s organisers were suspended beforehand, as were internet services in haryana & punjab. the government also shows no signs of regret as till now no public apology has been made, and no justifications given. rather, to add insult to injury, an order for another 30,000 tear gas shells was placed by the delhi police on the same day. in circumstances like these, where the government itself is doing very little to save face, with the bare minimum of even pr strategies (to be discussed in part two) one would expect public outrage more than or at least close to that during the 2021 protest (which was already not extreme, & this time’s response is far more intensive). instead, what is being observed across the nation, particularly among the residents of the capital, is widespread hostility. what started with a surprising amount of apathy has soon turned into an even more surprising amount of disgust, resentment, & vitriol against farmers. interviews conducted by the tve team within bustling markets & residential areas of the city reveal a disturbing reality: the ‘lying government’ is no longer the common man’s enemy, but anyone who opposes it; even if it’s another common man like himself. parents of children in board grades were concerned about traffic jams during their children’s papers. borders blockages & disturbed traffic flow for people who commute in & out of the city have become matters of inconvenience, yet who they hold accountable is not the government who's taking these decisions but the protesters who are ‘compelling’ it to. there seems to be a collective amnesia over the fact that delhi is not just the capital of the middle class in & around ncr but everyone, everywhere within the political boundary of this nation. that ‘chalo dilli’ has represented dissent, dignity, & being heard for none other than the common men who are silenced elsewhere in the country since before india was even a sovereign state. ‘ aane do inhe delhi, seedha goli maar denge. seedha goli maar deni chahiye inhe,’ (‘let them come to the capital, we will shoot them on sight. they should be shot on sight.’) said a shopkeeper in dwarka. he runs a small business with his family & likes to watch political youtube videos. he is a man of faith & sells photographs of gods & goddesses for a living. he is a kind man. what changed? what did the farmers do to them? what has made these normal, god-fearing men & women turn against their own kind so suddenly? when did farmers become the enemy? unsubtle influence: news & mass media large part of the answer is big & small-scale news reporting, trends, approaches, & subtle quirks of language that are all quantifiably effective tools for public perception control. viewers & readers need to understand that what the media & information industry performs is not just an act of ‘dissemination’ but also that of determination. there is a formalized structure to the creation of public perception, leading to the formation of something called the public sphere. simply put, your opinion has never really been entirely your own. while it might be ideal for every citizen to know at least the basics, it is ultimately a fact that components & dynamics of the public sphere are not common knowledge. (read next week: critical theory for the layman: why news media hides its workings from the common man) this is no coincidence; the lack of transparency in the workings of mass communication models is in fact by design & the reason why they are so effective in directing public opinion. the next section will explain, without lingo or jargon, what precisely these workings are with regard to the farmers' protest. ‘protesters or rioters?’ the problem with tv news post friday, farmers stated that they were afraid to clash with the ‘brute force’ the government is using against them, deploying paramilitary forces as if they are ‘the enemy.’ they do not wish to clash with the government , sarwan singh pandher, one of the key movement leaders, said. they just want their demands met. the march is a 'peaceful protest.' the march was again put on hold, awaiting another round of negotiations on sunday. “when the meetings have started, if we move forward (towards delhi) then how will meetings happen?" (movement leader jagjit singh dallewal, charushree chundawat, zee business). update, 20th february 2024 : as of 20th february, another round of negotiations has failed , & the march resumes. internet shutdowns in punjab & haryana have not been lifted, nor have border blockages. having established this timeline of events as it has taken place at several of delhi’s borders, we must now look at the trajectory of its presentation & coverage in mainstream media & public perception. consider india today’s broadcast of footage from the shambhu border, titled “protesters or rioters?” referring to visible agitation there, after haryana police had fired teargas shells at unarmed civilian protesters. a pointwise discussion of farmers pelting stones at the policemen standing atop vans & armory, and vandalizing safety barriers as a 'show of strength' was all the segment had to go on about as justification of the agenda, yet there were no questions raised about the policemen themselves 'inciting a riot' when the subject of them pelting stones back at farmers came up. a part of the crowd attempting to dismantle a safety barrier that showed it falling on top of them was discussed only as a humiliating failure of an out-of-control mob, rather than anything warranting sympathy or safety concern. this is by & large the approach that tv news channels have adopted in discussing matters of police violence toward farmers at the borders. it seems as if the very act of protesting strips you of all dignity & humanity, & thus being treated inhumanely by the government is not only acceptable but understood. their humiliation & injury are to be celebrated; their victories & competence are to be painted as acts of organised terror. billionaires, congress goons, & khalistanis: branding & prejudice we’ll club unintentionally satirical & cartoonish news channels (see: capital tv: chalo delhi 2.0 live: farmers protest 2024 or a khalistani agenda, know the truth | dr. manish kumar ) under the subhead of political commentators & miscellaneous opinion leaders in part two. for now, our assessment of public perception is concerned with the influence of formal & traditional news media, which follows at least structural if not ethical tenets of news production, & is taken seriously within the industry. an analysis of youtube comments under india today’s ‘protesters or rioters ’ broadcast revealed that large-scale support for farmers in the indian diaspora has been replaced with the same prejudiced ideas that they had so harshly rejected the state for propagating 3 years ago, along with an added desire to see these men violently penalised, from the celebration of the militant attacks to demands for expulsion of these individuals to ‘canada’ or ‘pakistan.’ the hatred is communally charged & hungry to see the protesters hurt, with some even criticising the modi regime for going too soft on them. “shameful comments in this forum. calling farmers terrorists and more is a disgrace. farmers all over north india in many states are protesting yet the media focus is on punjab!! punjabis are on the forefront just as punjabis were on the forefront of fighting foreign invaders from alexander to the mughals. these people are not terrorists, far from!!” supportive comments, though rare, can be found. but the unfortunate reality is that most of them come from the targeted community itself, defending, & not disagreeing. there are three primary assumptions that hostile audiences seem to be making about the protesters, with every farmer involved in the chalo dilli andolan being one, some or all of the following, all contributing to a larger narrative that feels more ‘anti-punjabi’ than anything else: khalistanis, i.e. separatist sikh people who want a sovereign nation for the punjabi-sikh community within present indian territory. goons in bed with the opposition, the one in power in punjab being the indian national congress. ‘millionaire’ farmers, or less radically understood to be landowners as opposed to cultivators, unaffected by farm laws & agricultural policy. as of yet, there is no linkage of any of the three farmers’ groups involved in the process with ‘khalistan’ advocates, nor with terrorist groups. their involvement with congress is obvious speculation, which albeit natural, still lacks evidential basis. given the intensive crackdown on the social media accounts & internet activities of those involved in or actively supporting the protest, large-scale or organised views of the country's agricultural masses have been shut down using british era laws, which does no favours to the idea that the farmers complaints are anyhow disingenuous. on the contrary, nationwide participation in strikes like the bharat bandh which are a show of solidarity, suggests the opposite. 2021 vs 2024: same players, new attitudes it is important to note that, while hints & leads to these ideas may be found in the reportage of most news outlets, due to the striking groundlessness of each, none of the points listed out in the report itself validated any of these claims explicitly. even government strategy has been a lot cleverer this time around, with spokesmen advertising diplomacy & violence hiding behind censorship & military policy. so what gives? consider the following report by india today during the previous farmer’s protest (see: bjp points at khalistani elements in farmers protest, jnu left-wing students have also joined stir ), a news channel whose reporting stance this time around has lent little sympathy to farmers, could then transparently interpret that 6 distinct individuals shouting separatist slogans at farmer’s rallies imply that the movement is disconnected from organisers of the ‘khalistani’ agenda rather than part of it, as alleged ‘khalistani elements’ seems to be attempting to either infiltrate or defame it from the outside. but even more surprising, is a look at the comments, 9 out of 12 of which were critical of the khalistani allegations & defended farmers. “no khalistani elements. the govt. failed to understand the demands of poor farmers.” “poor farmers are beaten by police.” in contrast, the majority of the (coherent) comments this time around are: “these are not farmers, the nation knows their intentions. all these guys are millionaires.” “my prayers go out to these policemen. please be safe while braving these so-called farmers.” “corretion - khalistan protests 2.0” (sic) “check these farmers' backgrounds. they could be abduls and ibrahims in the guise of taqiya singhs and harami singhs.” “these punjab farmers are a nuisance. while other state farmers are busy working hard. these punjab farmers are destroying public property.” communal prejudice & slurs litter these comment sections. public theories are always more conspiracy than fact, hate speeches seldom contain citations, & at the end of the day, people do have a right to speculate. but hatred, like empathy, does not come from vacuum. nothing does (read: hitler's propaganda ministry: news is not what you think it is). even seemingly outlandish ideas are carefully engineered, whether intentionally or unintentionally. the opinions of those labeling all turban-wearing, tractor-driving farmers with communal slurs & vitriol are not entirely their own, just like those labeling them victims of a capitalist regime. you are a product of what you read, see & hear, & while there are aspects of choice to this exercise, the freedom is mostly illusory. consider the following example: below is a brief description of the nightly distribution of supplies by ration trucks during the first week of the farmers’ protest: despite the brutality & lack of support they’ve been met with (except by opposition parties like congress who have predictably taken a pro-kisaan anti-bjp stance), the farmers weather on. 2021’s ‘chalo dilli march’ was a victory, not only for farmers but for commoners of the entire nation, as the government finally repealed its 3 controversial farm laws after the year-long protest. but this victory did not come easy. a year-long protest on the roads of delhi outskirts meant nights spent out in the december-january freezing temperatures & afternoons spent out during loo season. by the end of the year, 248 farmers had lost their lives , including 8 who were killed. lessons from the 2021 protests have made the farmers better equipped for what is to come. they are prepared this time around, having brought trucks of food supplies & blankets that are nightly distributed among protest members; a community taking care of its own. the wounded & injured are tended to in these hours, patched up & rested for another day of fighting. now consider the fact that the same visuals of food & blanket distribution were broadcast on indian news channels with voiceovers of khalistani & anti-punjabi rhetoric. the same clips doing the rounds on mainstream channels as well as more small tv networks broadcast these for entire lengths of programs, somehow managing to frame these men, many of them aged, all of them exhausted, as national security threats for eating food & taking care of each other. these are not luxuries. media perception & pseudointellectual attacks on the integrity of the movement seem to imply that a paper plate containing a handful of rice & spilling over dal is the height of decadence that these supposed ‘kulaks,’ greedy, rich landlords hailing from punjab are rewarding themselves with, blankets & tractors being evidence of their hoarded riches. opinion articles in the present media sphere, written by civilians without necessary journalistic or academic qualifications, reflect this mentality. those involved in the ongoing protest own tractors and harvesters, luxury goods that are not available to poor farm workers. they are allied with rich middlemen who are known as arhtiyas in northern india. they are already in a business where they are guaranteed a buyer and a minimum price for their principal products. in other words, the normal risks of business are reduced quite substantially for them. now, they are looking for guaranteed offtakes and prices for all their products. they also want state-funded crop insurance cover to pretty much eliminate their risks. and they want the state to provide a monthly pension of rs 10,000 a month to all farmers and agricultural labourers over 60, without farm owners making any contributions, unlike other businesses. one cannot blame the landlord-farmers for agitating. if they can arm-twist the rest of us taxpayers and get their way, why not? jaithirth ‘jerry rao for the print, why is india's left backing rich landlord-farmers? rao is the founder of mphasis, & currently owns the private equity firm, home finance first, a company whose market cap as of 2023 is rs. 6247 cr. parts of the population that have lived out not only their lives but entire generations without facing or being part of any political conflict now stand to opinionate on & dismiss a national protest as a convenient act of leisurely destruction. forgetting that hooligans don’t stick around to face teargas & rubber bullets, & neither do millionaires. millionaires, like jerry rao, sit in their air-conditioned ceo quarters & read profit reports of the quarter in crs while
