88: what does a precedent for such judicial amendments mean for the common man? a pil challenging the validity of rule 5 of up’s higher judicial service rules, 1975, in the allahabad high court, has brought under scrutiny its 2023 amendment & courts’ increasingly convenient interference with judicial regulation, whose notification was just issued this january. the following article explains why amendments like these affect more than just lawyers & judges, what the common man has at stake, & why speculation over why & how these decisions are taken is necessary to keep lawmaking powers accountable & in check. up’s higher judicial service rules, 1975 the uttar pradesh judicial service rules, 1975, is a short super session document laying down 34 rules first made by the governor of up in 1975. this was for ‘regulating the recruitment and appointment to the uttar pradesh higher judicial service and conditions of service and of persons appointed thereto.’ constitutionally, this power (to dictate & amend these rules) is granted to state governors by article 309 & article 233, the latter of which specifically discusses the appointment of district judges, providing that these rules be made in consultation with the respective high courts of the states. these articles, in accordance with which the rules are written, are a brief & recommended read, attached at the end of the article. the judiciary in india is a fast-evolving organism, following something called, an ‘adversarial’ model of law, which in simple terms reabsorbs every judicial decision taken back into its basis for taking the ones that are to come. this is why it only makes sense that the rules governing a higher judiciary, which one can argue need to take into account its changing precedent, must also be subject to change. but neither of these articles explicitly describes a model for the amendment of such legislature, leaving room for an ambiguity within which this pil resides. the 2023 amendment what was changed? from livelaw.in’s summary of rule 5 of u.p. higher judicial service rules, 1975 as amended in the year 2023 with the issuance of the notification dated 11th january 2024: rule 5 of the u.p. higher judicial service rules, 1975 provides for sources of recruitments in high judiciary. prior to amendment sub-rule (c) of rule 5 provided that for direct recruitment from amongst advocates, it was necessary to have a standing of not less than 7 years as on the last date fixed for submission of the application form. by amendment notification dated 11th january 2024, sub-rule (c) was amended to the extent that the words “practicing as an advocate” replaced the word “standing.” upasana agarwal, 2023 this refers to the following change: rule 5, sub-rule c, pre-amendment: “ by direct recruitment from amongst the advocates of not less than seven years standing on the first day of january next following the year in which the notice inviting applications is published. ” rule 5, sub-rule c, post-amendment: “ by direct recruitment from amongst the advocates who have been, for not less than seven years, practicing as an advocate, as on the last date fixed for the submission of application forms; provided that only such advocates shall be permitted to appear in the examination process who have been engaged independently for conducting not less than 30 cases (other than bunch cases) for unreserved categories and 24 cases (other than bunch cases) for scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and other backward classes in the preceding three years, from the year of publication of advertisement for recruitment, before any court. the certificate of such independent engagement may be issued by district & sessions judge of the district or registrar general/registrar of high courts or secretary general of supreme court, as the case may be .” (sic) read upasana agarwal’s full report of the case here. what does this mean in layman's terms? essentially, the rules now dictate that for the direct recruitment of district & sessions judges, it is necessary for them to have been in practice for no less than 7 years, while merely having the standing of advocate for the same duration would have sufficed before. this focus on quantifiable experience is further emphasised by the addition of a proviso that, in addition to this 7 years of continuous practice, also requires applicants to have been certifiably engaged in 30 independent cases (24 for reserved categories). the change that this will bring about is to pull more active lawyers into the courts as judges, & disqualify those who have merely been making the cut due to holding the title of ‘advocate’ as opposed to actively participating. is the 2023 amendment good or bad? in effect, this amendment makes the eligibility criteria for district & sessions judges more stringent, & in this regard can only serve to improve the legal service & justice that civilians receive. the concerned features amended & added are both relevant, as legal practice in india is a continuously evolving bureaucratic process, & evidence of recent & consistent participation is a legitimate question of qualification for a higher court judge; it makes the difference between being competent & out of touch. ‘it changes things,because obviously, you would prefer a judge who has been practising for 7 years, rather than someone who's just waited 7 years after acquiring the title & doesn't have any real experience.’ jia ahuja, a journalist specialising in information property law, told tve. so what is the problem? how does this simple, reasonable amendment, ‘violate the constitution’? why is there a pil against this change? the problem arises not from what the amendment changes, but how. petitioner trideep narayan pandey's case consists of four core arguments, all boiling down to the same principle. it wasn't done the right way. why is an authority whose power to influence lawmaking about its own structural & recruitment procedure is only vaguely stipulated in the constitution, actively recommending amendments to pre-existing legislature? another argument put forth by pandey’s counsel was with of sub-rule c (refer to earlier section), calling it ‘arbitrary’ & in violation of article 14 of the indian constitution (‘ the state shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of india .’) both of these arguments were disputed in the honourable court’s proceedings on the 7th of february, where the defending counsel brought forth an obvious conflict of interest of the petitioner, with pandey himself being an aspirant of the higher judicial services. against the claims of constitutional violations, it argued that constitutional articles should not be looked at in ‘isolation’ & that the indian constitution holistically supports & encourages the high court's authority in making legal recommendations. largely, the defending counsel dismissed the petition as lacking ‘legal sanctity,’ & both parties have now been given time to exchange affidavits. discussion: how much power do the courts really have? as those who recall cbse’s sixth-grade civics curriculum would remember, india's governance & political order is one that functions on the principle of ‘checks & balances.’ a separation of the judiciary from the legislature & the executive is fundamental to this principle. the second reasoning defending the amendment fails to acknowledge that there is a reason why the constitution upon ‘holistic reading’ appears to legitimise court-given ‘recommendations’ to legislative policy, with the specific exception of the two articles concerning lawmaking about courts themselves, & is almost covert in attempting to distract from this obvious catch. even if the first claim stands true, & the petitioner's motives are ulterior, the same conflict of interest that is being used to defend the amendment is also found within the very act of a high court taking control of its own regulation policy. what is noteworthy about this case is not so much the actual change enacted, but rather the simple, effortless nature of the process that led to it; quiet & unnoticed. the state’s defense & casual dismissal of a question raised over its jurisdiction seems to imply an understood normalization of such an initiative. it is acknowledged that there is a gap in the constitutional framework where there should be a provision for legislative amendment of judicial regulation as opposed to just initiation, & it not only leaves open room for but necessitates external direction. but does it have to be the judiciary to take it upon itself to fill this gap? has it already been for a long time? should it be? just how much power does the judiciary really have, if such interpretation goes unchallenged? just how regulated are the self-regulated? read for yourself: 87: julius caesar and his many jeopardies i first came across the name, julius caesar, while flitting through the pages of my middle school textbook three quarters of a decade ago. the great roman ruler, romanticized in the words of shakespeare, painted a somewhat sympathetic picture in my mind. a man slayed by his own; how could one not feel pity? i was young and impressionable, taking william's affinity for drama to be mortal truth. julius therefore did enjoy a high position (heh) in my mind for a couple of years. now that i am older, i feel obligated to hold myself accountable. outside of fiction, julius caesar was just a general who later became rome's self-proclaimed elected leader. his troops marched forward to conquer the gallic tribes while mercilessly exploiting tribal rivalries. it inevitably led to the infamous and much talked about civil war between caesar’s gallant forces and his arch nemesis, pompey. while caesar emerged victorious, he reserved for himself a feeling of hatred in the hearts of many. enough for those many to plot his downfall and eventually ensure it. he tasted the sweet fruit of victory but - as they say in middle school english textbooks - alas, he couldn't enjoy it. a mere 5 years into the rule, he was assassinated with a dagger (& then several more) through the heart by those he trusted most. and the question that both thespians & newsreaders of 44 bc have deigned to haunt us with forever, is did he deserve it? what comes to mind when hearing the word 'dictator' is normatively defined. cruel, evil, merciless - the worst person ever. but its etymology is fairly neutral. it derives, obviously, from the term 'dictate,' i.e. 'to tell someone what to do.' a dictator as a political role then, in essence, is little more than managerial. its only association to popular history is that the exemplary work of dictators like stalin, hitler, and kim jong-un has managed to paint a prevailing mindset that dictators are inherently awful and malevolent individuals, and that much is fine. but then you see mustafa kemal, fondly known as atatürk - ' father of the turks, ' a revolutionary nationalist who rose against the ottoman empire in the early 20th century and led turkey on a path of modernization. you see lee kuan yew, who led singapore to independence from british rule in 1959 and elevated its agricultural economy to new heights, laying the foundation for singapore to become one of asia's wealthiest countries. you see more & you read more & you're forced to ask - what gives? the modern geo-political world has afforded too much importance to words and labels. a young girl who likes video games becomes an nlog becomes a pick-me. a terrorist becomes a prime minister becomes a gold medalist becomes a world leader. a ceo becomes a genius becomes revolutionary becomes a meme. invaders become natives become civilized become developed. the indian state of allahabad becomes the bharatiya state of prayagraj. it seems that nouns, even proper ones, now carry the potential to alter the course of history. perhaps, before anything else, the dictator is a victim of semiotics. which of our polities is a democracy & which a dictatorship is perhaps more a function of aesthetics than it ever was of social science. perhaps caesar wasn't the first dictator, so much as he was simply the first so called, and perhaps (perhaps), this is what shakespeare meant, when he asked what is in a name. proposed by kashvi basu, the voice express .

portrayals & their being found increasingly in children's media & educational material may appear harmless & at most, hilarious, due to its contrast with the buffoonish & mockable image of modi that older audiences default to, but is as sinister if not more than any other structural parallel observed here. it is here that the construction of the 'myth' (the leader, the führer, the son of the 68: published in 1944 under the pseudonym mary westmacott, "absent in the spring" is a book by agatha christie. the title has been taken from william shakespeare's sonnet 98, "from you have i been absent in the spring.” the significance of spring is not being able to enjoy the blooming season when a loved one is not there. in contrast to her well-known detective stories, this book offers a psychological exploration of joan scudamore, a woman who finds herself left alone in the desert and forced to face her actual nature. in the 1940s, a middle-aged woman named joan scudamore makes a solo trip from baghdad to kirkuk to visit her husband, who works for an oil company. she is stranded in her home for a few days because of a sudden sandstorm, and during that time, she starts to think back on her relationships and life. she learns that she has been so preoccupied with trying to satisfy other people and fit in with social norms that she has lost sight of her own wants and individuality. joan comes to the realization that she has been portraying a fake self to everyone, even her own family, and has been living a lie. when she starts to accept who she really is, joan's epiphany is both upsetting and empowering. the book is exquisitely written and displays christie's talent for telling tales. it digs into the intricacies of interpersonal interactions and the challenges of comprehending one's own emotions and intentions. readers will identify with joan's complex and likable character as she attempts to understand her inner conflicts. in conclusion, "absent in the spring" is a challenging and touching book that differs from christie's typical detective stories yet is no less engrossing. for admirers of christie's writing and anyone interested in learning more about the human condition, it is a must-read.

aashirvad aatta equivalent rifle dummies carried out the section attack on the front lawns (“arrowhead formation” “classic”) as a crowd consisting of 30-person teams along with their moral supporters of over 23 institutions (including those from outside of the directorate) surrounded the grounds looking anywhere but at them. culture finds a way. it is a reasonable claim to make - albeit still a claim - that it is ultimately not alienation or ignorance but familiarity that breeds apathy. an observation that at the end of the day seemed more worthwhile a subject to write down this piece of pseudo-news about than any number of lacklustre open ground concerts where the noise is too loud, the food stalls too desperate and the number on the cheque cashed by the artist too long was simply this: the world is recursive. arvind kejriwal used a phrase in his speech at the directorate general of ncc on the 8th of january at this year’s cm visit for the republic day celebrations: “[] a microcosm of the country.” but a national integration camp is not what is a microcosm and our nation is not what it is a microcosm of. the world is recursive. society recreates itself within itself, and whether it be an unmoving resilience of the human spirit or a biological vulnerability to the goddamn sound of bleating, a man will create tradition where he cannot find it, if only so he has something to get used to. the various niches of du fests - departmental, eca, ncc, nss, what have you - are a case study in self-sustaining ecosystems. a ”normal” person walking into the gates of cadet’23 (excellent name, by the way, truly an epitome of the spirit of originality and creativity the military and modern education are so insistent upon inculcating) will find certain sights to gaze upon. goats in a petting zoo. infiltrators in a cult. look how they greet each other, arms a stiff set by their sides, white lie caressing their lips (“ jai hind everyone ”). look what they care about, creases on their pants and 3 buttons over their waists. look how they think; they don’t. somewhere past the point of no return of zoning out on the rifles aimed directly between my eyes as the section attack droned on, my friend had thrust a green piece of sponge and a white bottle of shoeshine into my hands. multipurpose polish, that’s what she’d called it. “what, seriously?” “seriously.” “fuck off.” she’d just given me a look, then took the polish back and started brute-forcing the last of it out onto the sponge. i rolled my eyes and moved to a ledge nearby, waving her to come over. the front crease of the uniform is as delicate as it is permanent. you can’t be bending over in half 30 minutes from your inspection, and a shoe has to shine. unfortunately for her, by the time she’d managed to get a millimetre of her multipurpose polish out onto her flimsy dish sponge and walk over to me another of her subordinates had beat her to it (you shine one guy’s shoes, you shine the whole squad’s). one who had several complaints to make about my shoe-shining skills. “maybe just polish it yourself then. she’s doing it, isn’t she?” “yeah i’m doing it, just shut the fuck up.” “that’s enough! i’ll do it,” said my friend. owner of and first in line for the polish, and incidentally, the junior under officer of our company. the senior most in our batch. “no, you can’t,” the whiner said. took her shoe off the ledge. “put it back up.” “please don’t.” “what did i say?” for the life of that dying bottle, dear old juo managed to polish every single one of those 9 pairs of drill march shoes, some better than others. she stood there frowning beside me after the formality of brushing a dry sponge over her own shoes and wordlessly handed her precious materials back over to me. “this is pretty wet,” i’d said then. silence. “probably still has a substantial amount of polish in it.” i lent over and pressed the last dredges of multipurpose shoeshine onto her dust-covered boots. best i could. “it works on normal shoes, too.” “that’s nice.” “i said, it works on normal shoes, too .” i looked up at her and her eyes moved down to my shoes and back to me. she raised an eyebrow. i rolled my eyes and pressed the sponge down on my own no longer black sport shoes. she smiled. “see?” “i do.” “it’s useful, isn’t it.” “they don’t need polish, dude they need a turbo wash.” “yeah, but if you polished them you wouldn’t have to turbo wash them.” i gave her a look. she smiled. there is a certain isomorphism to self-contained social subsystems that will go over the head of anyone lost to the great big symbolism of the shoe. a good leader in an ncc fest leading a squad drill team is the same as one in a hackathon is the same as one in band is the same as the one on the council, even if their languages don’t translate. did you go to school with the same people you met at college? are you working with the same people you sit with at dinner? do you want to? you move past the arrogance of believing yourself to be more than the common indian idiot, and you’ll realize that the eccentricities you find voyeurising the unbent knees and the abdominal cry of a military squad are just variants of your own. you are guilty of worship, you’ve just given your god a different name. you are the cult and you are the petting zoo. your normalcy is an illusion. the best you can hope for in life is people you’d douse your sports shoes in wax for. a multipurpose polish that works on all kinds of shoes. a dummy rifle that slaps back. a tug of war rope that isn’t long enough. good fest or bad fest because everything everyone everywhere is the same. the best you can hope for is to find something you cannot predict.
